t: 1A.2 Introduction: what a network actually does
c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: A network moves data from one program on one device to another program on another device. When you open a website on your laptop in Birgunj, your browser hands a request to your laptop's network software. That software wraps the request in addressing information, turns it into electrical signals or radio waves, and sends it to the next device. Every device on the path reads only the information it needs, then passes the data on. Networking models exist so that this job is split into layers. Each layer solves one problem and trusts the layers below it. Cable makers do not need to know about web browsers, and browser developers do not need to know about cables.

c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: The OSI model has seven layers and is used to talk about problems ("it's a Layer 1 issue"). The TCP/IP model is the one the Internet actually runs on. You need to map between them quickly. Exam tip When the exam says "Layer 2 problem", think MAC addresses, VLANs, trunks, STP. "Layer 3 problem" means IP addressing, subnet masks, default gateways, routing. Memory trick Now bottom-up, layers 1 → 7: P lease D o N ot T hrow S ausage P izza A way — Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: Encapsulation means each layer adds its own header (and Ethernet also adds a trailer) in front of the data it receives from the layer above. Decapsulation is the reverse on the receiving side. Figure 1.1 shows PC1 sending a web request; Figure 1.2 then follows the frame across the switch and the router. Figure 1.1 Encapsulation: each TCP/IP layer adds its header to the data on the way down The data block (highlighted) never changes on the way down; each layer only adds its header, and Data Link also adds the FCS trailer. The receiver reads the same picture bottom to top, removing one header per layer. Sending (PC1 → web server at 203.0.113.80): The browser creates an HTTP request (Application data). Transport adds a TCP header: source port 50123 (random, chosen by PC1), destination port 443 (HTTPS). The result is a segment . Network adds an IPv4 header: source 10.10.10.11, destination 203.0.113.80. The result is a packet . Data Link adds an Ethernet header and trailer. The destination MAC is the default gateway's MAC (R1), not the web server's, because the server is on another network. The result is a frame . Physical turns the frame into bits on the wire. Receiving (R1, the router): R1 receives bits, rebuilds the frame and checks the FCS (error check). A bad FCS means the frame is dropped and the CRC counter rises — this is why cable faults show up as CRC errors. R1 sees its own MAC as destination, removes the Ethernet header, and reads the IP destination. R1 looks up 203.0.113.80 in its routing table, then builds a new Ethernet frame for the next link. The IP addresses stay the same end to end; the MAC addresses change at every hop (unless NAT is used, Chapter 21). Figure 1.2 Hop-by-hop forwarding: MAC addresses are rewritten by R1, IP addresses are not In Figure 1.2 the arrows show the direction of travel. SW1 forwards the frame unchanged because it only reads the destination MAC. R1 strips the old Ethernet header and builds a new one for the next link, while the IP header keeps the same source and destination. Memory trick PDU names from Layer 4 down: S ome P eople F ear B irthdays — Segment, Packet, Frame, Bits.

c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: A MAC address is 48 bits, written as 12 hexadecimal digits, for example 0050.7966.6801 (Cisco style) or 00-50-79-66-68-01 (Windows style). The first 24 bits are the OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier), which identifies the manufacturer; the last 24 bits are assigned by that manufacturer. Type Destination MAC Who receives it Unicast One device's MAC That device only Broadcast FFFF.FFFF.FFFF Every device in the VLAN (e.g. ARP requests, DHCP Discover) Multicast Starts 0100.5E (IPv4) or 3333 (IPv6) Devices that joined that group (e.g. OSPF hellos) Ethernet II frame layout (sizes in bytes) Field Size Purpose Preamble + SFD 7 + 1 Synchronises the receiver's clock; not counted in frame size Destination MAC 6 Where the frame goes on this link Source MAC 6 Who sent it on this link 802.1Q tag (only on trunks) 4 VLAN ID and priority (Chapter 5) Type 2 Payload protocol: 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP Payload 46–1500 The packet; 1500 bytes is the standard MTU FCS 4 CRC checksum; a mismatch = corrupted frame, dropped A normal Ethernet frame is therefore 64 to 1518 bytes (1522 with an 802.1Q tag). Frames smaller than 64 bytes are runts ; frames larger than the maximum are giants . Both counters appear in show interfaces and matter for objective 1.1. Figure 1.3 Ethernet II frame layout with field sizes and purposes (fields not drawn to scale) Figure 1.3 shows the same fields as the table above, in transmission order from left to right. The highlighted payload is the IP packet from Figure 1.1 ; everything from Destination MAC to FCS counts toward the 64–1518-byte frame size.

c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: A switch builds its MAC address table by watching source addresses. Learn: a frame arrives on Fa0/1 from 0050.7966.6801 . The switch records "this MAC is on Fa0/1, VLAN 1" (entries age out after 300 seconds by default). Forward: if the destination MAC is in the table, the frame goes out only that port. Flood: if the destination is unknown, broadcast or (by default) multicast, the frame goes out every port in the same VLAN except the one it came in. Filter: if the destination is on the same port it arrived on, the frame is dropped. Figure 1.4 Switch frame-forwarding logic: learn, then flood, filter or forward Figure 1.4 runs once for every frame. Learning always uses the source address; the forwarding choice always uses the destination address. Unknown multicast is flooded like a broadcast by default. SW1 Copy commands SW1# show mac address-table dynamic Mac Address Table ------------------------------------------- Vlan Mac Address Type Ports ---- ----------- -------- ----- 1 0050.7966.6801 DYNAMIC Fa0/1 1 0050.7966.6802 DYNAMIC Gi0/1 Read it as: PC1's MAC lives behind Fa0/1; the second MAC is reached through the uplink Gi0/1, so that host is on another switch. Collision domain vs broadcast domain. A collision domain is the set of devices whose transmissions can collide; on a modern switch with full-duplex ports each port is its own, and collisions should be zero. A broadcast domain is the set of devices that receive each other's broadcasts; one VLAN is one broadcast domain, and routers stop broadcasts. ARP in one paragraph. Before PC1 can send to 10.10.10.1 it needs that IP's MAC address. PC1 broadcasts an ARP Request ("who has 10.10.10.1?"); R1 replies by unicast with its MAC; PC1 caches it ( arp -a on Windows shows the cache). If a host's gateway or mask is wrong, ARP is often where the fault first appears.

c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: A cable fault rarely looks like a cable fault. A duplex mismatch keeps the link up but makes file transfers crawl. A cable that is 130 m long may come up but show CRC errors all day. A fiber patch lead with swapped strands shows no light at all. Your job is to collect evidence — status, counters, logs, optical readings — and match it to a cause.

t: 1B.3 Copper cabling: categories, standards and distance
c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: Ethernet over copper uses UTP (unshielded twisted pair) : four twisted pairs in one jacket, ending in RJ-45 connectors. Twisting cancels electromagnetic interference (EMI); untwisting too much at the connector causes crosstalk and errors. STP/FTP (shielded) cable is used near heavy EMI such as motors. Standard (common name) IEEE Speed Minimum cable Max distance Pairs used 10BASE-T (Ethernet) 802.3i 10 Mb/s Cat3 100 m 2 (pins 1,2 and 3,6) 100BASE-TX (Fast Ethernet) 802.3u 100 Mb/s Cat5 100 m 2 (pins 1,2 and 3,6) 1000BASE-T (Gigabit Ethernet) 802.3ab 1 Gb/s Cat5e 100 m All 4 pairs, both directions 10GBASE-T 802.3an 10 Gb/s Cat6a (Cat6 up to 55 m) 100 m All 4 pairs The 100 m rule covers the whole channel: typically 90 m of permanent cable plus patch leads. Beyond it, signals weaken and pick up noise, so you see CRC and input errors, a link that flaps up and down, or a link that only negotiates at a lower speed.

t: 1B.4 Pinouts: T568A, T568B, straight-through, crossover, rollover
c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: The two wiring standards differ only by swapping the green and orange pairs. Pin T568A T568B 10/100 role on a PC/router (MDI) 1 White/green White/orange Transmit + 2 Green Orange Transmit − 3 White/orange White/green Receive + 4 Blue Blue (used by 1000BASE-T) 5 White/blue White/blue (used by 1000BASE-T) 6 Orange Green Receive − 7 White/brown White/brown (used by 1000BASE-T) 8 Brown Brown (used by 1000BASE-T) Why cable type matters. PCs, routers, servers, firewalls and APs are MDI devices: they transmit on pins 1,2 and receive on 3,6. Switches (and hubs) are MDI-X : they do the opposite. Transmit must meet receive. Cable Wiring Use between Examples Straight-through Same standard both ends (B–B) Unlike devices (MDI ↔ MDI-X) PC–switch, router–switch, AP–switch Crossover A one end, B the other Like devices (MDI ↔ MDI, MDI-X ↔ MDI-X) Switch–switch, PC–PC, router–router, PC–router Rollover (console) Pins reversed 1↔8 PC serial/USB to device console port Initial setup, password recovery Figure 1.6 Straight-through and crossover pin mapping for 10/100 Ethernet (MDI vs MDI-X) Figure 1.6 , left: a PC sends on pins 1 and 2 and the switch listens on 1 and 2, so the wires run straight. Right: two switches both listen on 1 and 2, so the cable must cross each side's 3/6 transmit pair over to the other side's 1/2 receive pair. Auto-MDIX lets a port detect the wrong cable and swap its own transmit and receive pairs. Most current Cisco switches enable it by default ( mdix auto ); on many models it only works when speed and duplex are both set to auto . Gigabit 1000BASE-T ports handle pair swapping as part of the standard. So on real modern gear a "wrong" cable often still works — but the exam still expects you to know the correct cable, and Packet Tracer often does not apply auto-MDIX , so the link stays red. Memory trick Sort devices into two teams: PCs and routers (MDI) and switches and hubs (MDI-X). Same team → crossover ; different teams → straight-through . The rollover cable is only for the console port.

c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: Fiber carries light, so it is immune to EMI, can run much further than copper, and is used for uplinks between floors and buildings. A fiber link uses two strands : one to transmit, one to receive. Tx on one end must connect to Rx on the other. Multimode fiber (MMF) Single-mode fiber (SMF) Core diameter 50 or 62.5 µm (cladding 125 µm) About 9 µm (cladding 125 µm) Light source LED or VCSEL laser Laser Light paths Many modes bounce through the core One mode, straight path Typical distance Hundreds of metres Kilometres (10 km and beyond) Cost Cheaper optics More expensive optics Jacket colour (convention) Orange (OM1/OM2), aqua (OM3/OM4) Yellow Figure 1.7 Multimode vs single-mode fiber: core size, light source and light paths Figure 1.7 shows why reach differs. In the wide multimode core, light takes several zig-zag paths of different lengths, so a pulse spreads out over distance. The narrow single-mode core allows only one path, so the pulse stays sharp for kilometres. Standard Fiber Typical reach 1000BASE-SX MMF About 220–550 m depending on fiber grade 1000BASE-LX/LH SMF (also MMF with conditioning) 5–10 km depending on optic 10GBASE-SR MMF About 300 m on OM3, 400 m on OM4 10GBASE-LR SMF 10 km Reach figures vary by optic model; always check the transceiver data sheet. Fiber ports usually take a pluggable transceiver : SFP (1 Gb/s), SFP+ (10 Gb/s), QSFP (40/100 Gb/s). Common connectors are LC (small, duplex, the usual one on SFPs) and SC (larger, square, push-pull). A mismatched optic is a cable-type fault. An SX optic on one end and an LX optic on the other, or an SR optic plugged into single-mode fiber, gives no link or a very weak signal.

t: 1B.6 Signal levels: reading optical power in dBm
c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: Optical power is measured in dBm (decibels relative to 1 milliwatt). 0 dBm = 1 mW. Every 3 dB lower roughly halves the power, so −3 dBm ≈ 0.5 mW and −10 dBm = 0.1 mW. More negative means weaker. Signal levels are the "signal levels" in objective 1.1. Transceivers with DOM (digital optical monitoring) report their readings: SW1 Copy commands SW1# show interfaces transceiver Optical Optical Temperature Voltage Current Tx Power Rx Power Port (Celsius) (Volts) (mA) (dBm) (dBm) --------- ----------- ------- ------- -------- -------- Gi1/1/1 33.1 3.29 6.2 -5.1 -6.8 Gi1/1/2 34.0 3.28 6.0 -5.3 -24.9 -- Gi1/1/1 is healthy: received power (−6.8 dBm) is close to what the far end transmits, so little light is being lost. Gi1/1/2 shows -- , meaning Rx power is below the low-alarm threshold . Suspects, in order: dirty or damaged connector, a tight bend or crushed fiber, wrong fiber type, too long a run, a faulty far-end optic. Rx too high (marked ++ ) happens when a long-range optic is used on a short single-mode run; the receiver is overloaded. The fix is an attenuator or a shorter-reach optic. No light at all on both ends: check that Tx and Rx are not swapped (or not both connected Tx-to-Tx). show interfaces transceiver detail prints the alarm and warning thresholds for each optic. Output format varies by platform, and not every optic supports DOM. PT note: Packet Tracer does not simulate optical power; learn this from the output above.

t: 1B.8 Speed and duplex: autonegotiation and mismatches
c: Chapter 1 · Networking foundations, cables and interfaces
x: Duplex is whether a link can send and receive at the same time. Full duplex can; collisions are impossible. Half duplex cannot; the device must listen first (CSMA/CD) and collisions are normal. Modern switched networks should be full duplex everywhere. Autonegotiation (IEEE 802.3u/802.3ab) lets both ends agree the best common speed and duplex. Problems start when only one side negotiates. What the negotiating side does if the other side is hard-coded: Speed: it can still detect the speed from the electrical signal, so speed is usually correct. Duplex: it cannot detect duplex, so it falls back to a default: half duplex at 10 or 100 Mb/s, full duplex at 1000 Mb/s . That is how a duplex mismatch is born: R1 is hard-coded to speed 100 and duplex full ; SW1 is left on auto, senses 100 Mb/s and falls back to half duplex. Fault Link status Evidence on the full-duplex side Evidence on the half-duplex side Users notice Duplex mismatch up/up CRC errors, runts, input errors Late collisions , collisions Slow, worse under load; pings may look fine Speed mismatch (both hard-coded differently) down/down (notconnect) — — No connectivity at all Figure 1.8 Duplex mismatch: how it forms and the evidence on each side of the link Figure 1.8 uses the same SW1–SW2 link as Lab 1.2. The highlighted SW2 port is where the problem is born: it negotiates, cannot learn the duplex, and falls back to half. Each side then records a different kind of error, so always compare counters on both ends. CDP also warns you about duplex mismatches: Copy %CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH: duplex mismatch discovered on GigabitEthernet0/1 (not full duplex), with SW2 GigabitEthernet0/1 (full duplex). Configuring speed and duplex (interface configuration mode): SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1 SW1(config-if)# description Uplink to SW2 Gi0/1 SW1(config-if)# speed 1000 ! options: 10 | 100 | 1000 | auto (platform-dependent) SW1(config-if)# duplex full ! options: half | full | auto SW1(config-if)# end Command Mode Purpose Common mistake speed {10\|100\|1000\|auto} Interface config Sets or negotiates speed Hard-coding one end only duplex {half\|full\|auto} Interface config Sets or negotiates duplex Same — set both ends identically, or leave both on auto mdix auto Interface config Enables auto-MDIX (switches) Expecting it to work after hard-coding speed/duplex on some models description <text> Interface config Documents the link Leaving it blank; descriptions speed up troubleshooting and help with CDP/LLDP validation (Chapter 8) Best practice Leave both ends on auto , or set both ends to the same speed and duplex. Never mix.

x: show interfaces is the most detailed Layer 1/2 command. On the far end (hard-coded full) you would see CRC errors and runts climbing. The 37 late collisions on this half-duplex side are the classic duplex-mismatch signature. Check both ends of the link. Administratively down? Enter no shutdown . err-disabled? Read show logging and show interfaces status err-disabled for the reason, fix it, then bounce the port with shutdown / no shutdown . down/down or notconnect? Check physically: cable seated, link lights, correct cable type (straight vs crossover in labs), cable length, far end enabled, matching speed settings, correct and matching transceivers, fiber Tx/Rx orientation, Rx light level. up/up but slow or dropping? Compare speed and duplex on both ends. Look at CRC, runts, collisions, late collisions. Clear counters and watch which ones rise. Counters clean but still failing? c: Chapter 2 · IPv4 addressing and subnetting
x: An IPv4 address works like a postal address: one part names the street (the network ), the other names the house (the host ). Routers only care about the street. The subnet mask or prefix length is what tells every device where the street name ends and the house number begins. Almost every IPv4 fault in the exam is a disagreement about that boundary.

c: Chapter 2 · IPv4 addressing and subnetting
x: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four 8-bit octets in decimal. Each bit position in an octet has a fixed place value : 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Add the place values where the bit is 1. Binary → decimal ( Figure 2.1 ): 10101100 = 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 = 172 . Figure 2.1 Octet place values: converting 10101100 to 172 In Figure 2.1 the highlighted cells are the 1 bits. Only their place values (128, 32, 8, 4) are added; every 0 bit contributes nothing. The same eight place values are used for every octet of every address. Decimal → binary , by subtraction. Convert 202: 202 ≥ 128? Yes → bit 1, remainder 74. 74 ≥ 64? Yes → bit 1, remainder 10. 10 ≥ 32? No → 0. 10 ≥ 16? No → 0. 10 ≥ 8? Yes → 1, remainder 2. 2 ≥ 4? No → 0. 2 ≥ 2? Yes → 1, remainder 0. 0 ≥ 1? No → 0. Result: 11001010 . The nine mask-octet values to memorise. A mask is a run of 1s followed by 0s, so each mask octet is the place values added from the left: Bits set Binary Decimal Block size (256 − value) 0 00000000 0 256 1 10000000 128 128 2 11000000 192 64 3 11100000 224 32 4 11110000 240 16 5 11111000 248 8 6 11111100 252 4 7 11111110 254 2 8 11111111 255 1 Any other number in a mask (for example 255.255.255.100) is invalid.

t: 2.4 IPv4 address structure, prefix length and mask
c: Chapter 2 · IPv4 addressing and subnetting
x: A prefix length (CIDR notation, for example /26 ) says how many leading bits are network bits. The subnet mask says the same thing in dotted decimal: /26 = 26 ones = 255.255.255.192 . The remaining bits (32 − 26 = 6) are host bits . Figure 2.2 shows 192.168.10.75/26 bit by bit. Figure 2.2 192.168.10.75/26 in binary: network bits, host bits, network and broadcast addresses In Figure 2.2 the shaded columns are the 26 network bits; they are identical in the address, the network address and the broadcast address. Only the last 6 host bits change: all 0s gives the network address, all 1s gives the broadcast. Three addresses every subnet has: Network address — all host bits 0. Names the subnet; used in routing tables; cannot be given to a host. Broadcast address — all host bits 1. Reaches every host in the subnet; cannot be given to a host. Usable hosts — everything between them. Count = 2^h − 2, where h = number of host bits. Two exceptions: a /31 has two addresses, and both are usable on point-to-point router links (RFC 3021). A /32 is a single address, used for loopbacks and host routes (Chapter 11). Address classes (historical, still used in vocabulary): Class First octet Default mask Purpose A 1–126 /8 (255.0.0.0) Large unicast networks B 128–191 /16 (255.255.0.0) Medium unicast networks C 192–223 /24 (255.255.255.0) Small unicast networks D 224–239 — Multicast E 240–255 — Experimental / reserved Modern networks are classless : any prefix length can be used with any address. Classes matter only because IOS and some exam questions still say "classful boundary".

t: 2.6 Calculating network, broadcast and host range
c: Chapter 2 · IPv4 addressing and subnetting
x: There are two methods. Learn the binary method so you understand it, then use the block-size method in the exam because it is faster. Method 1 — binary AND (always works). Worked example: 192.168.10.75/26. Write the address and mask in binary ( Figure 2.2 ). AND them bit by bit (1 AND 1 = 1, anything AND 0 = 0). Result: 11000000.10101000.00001010.01000000 = 192.168.10.64 — the network address. Set all 6 host bits to 1: ...01111111 = 192.168.10.127 — the broadcast. First usable host = network + 1 = 192.168.10.65 . Last usable = broadcast − 1 = 192.168.10.126 . Hosts = 2^6 − 2 = 62 . Method 2 — block size (the fast exam method). Find the interesting octet : the octet where the mask is neither 255 nor 0. For /26 that is the 4th octet (mask value 192). Block size = 256 − mask value = 256 − 192 = 64 . Subnets in that octet start at multiples of 64: 0, 64, 128, 192. Find the multiple at or below the address's value in that octet: 75 → 64 . That is the network address: 192.168.10. 64 . The next subnet starts at 64 + 64 = 128, so the broadcast is one less: 192.168.10. 127 . Octets to the left copy the address; octets to the right are 0 for the network and 255 for the broadcast. Figure 2.3 draws steps 2 and 3 on a number line. Figure 2.3 Dividing 192.168.10.0/24 into /26 blocks and locating host .75 Figure 2.3 shows the whole fourth octet (0–255) cut into four blocks of 64. The arrow marks host .75; it lands in the highlighted block, so its network is .64 and its broadcast is .127. The same method in the 3rd octet: 172.16.45.200/20. /20 → mask 255.255. 240 .0 → interesting octet is the 3rd; block size 256 − 240 = 16 . Multiples of 16 in the 3rd octet: 0, 16, 32, 48 ... 45 falls in the block starting at 32 . Network: 172.16.32.0 . Next block starts at 172.16.48.0, so broadcast: 172.16.47.255 . Usable: 172.16.32.1 to 172.16.47.254. Host bits = 32 − 20 = 12, so 2^12 − 2 = 4094 hosts. And in the 2nd octet: 10.200.77.9/12 → mask 255. 240 .0.0, block 16 in the 2nd octet, 200 falls in the block starting at 192 → network 10.192.0.0 , broadcast 10.207.255.255 , 2^20 − 2 = 1,048,574 hosts. Memory trick Magic number = 256 − the interesting octet of the mask. Subnets start at multiples of it; the broadcast is the next subnet minus one. Drill it until it is automatic in the subnetting practice game .

A host sends directly (via ARP) to any destination it believes is in its own subnet, and sends everything else to its default gateway. If the host's mask is wrong, it makes the wrong choice: it may ARP for a remote host that will never answer, or send a local packet to the router. That single rule explains most addressing faults in 2.11.

t: 2.8 Subnetting a block: by number of subnets or number of hosts
c: Chapter 2 · IPv4 addressing and subnetting
x: Subnetting means borrowing host bits to create more, smaller networks. Each borrowed bit doubles the number of subnets and roughly halves the hosts in each. Subnets created = 2^s, where s = bits borrowed. Hosts per subnet = 2^h − 2, where h = host bits left. By number of subnets. "Split 192.168.50.0/24 into at least 6 subnets." Smallest s with 2^s ≥ 6 is s = 3 (8 subnets). New prefix = /24 + 3 = /27 (mask 255.255.255.224); block size 32; hosts 2^5 − 2 = 30. Subnets: .0, .32, .64, .96, .128, .160, .192, .224 (each /27). Example: the third subnet is 192.168.50.64/27, usable .65–.94, broadcast .95. By number of hosts. "Each subnet needs 500 hosts." Smallest h with 2^h − 2 ≥ 500 is h = 9 (510 hosts). Prefix = 32 − 9 = /23 (255.255.254.0). Exam tip Always subtract 2 for hosts but never for subnets. A question asking for "at least 30 hosts" is satisfied by /27 (30), but "at least 31 hosts" needs /26 (62).

t: 2.9 VLSM: different-sized subnets from one block
c: Chapter 2 · IPv4 addressing and subnetting
x: Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) lets each subnet use the prefix that fits its size, instead of making every subnet as big as the largest. Rules: List the requirements and sort them largest first . For each, choose the smallest prefix that fits (hosts + 2 ≤ block). Allocate it at the next free address that is a multiple of its block size . Record the range, then continue with the next requirement. Worked example: one /24 for the Kathmandu branch. You have only 172.16.0.0/24. Requirements: Staff 100 hosts, Wireless 50, Printers/IoT 20, Management 10, two router-to-router links with 2 hosts each. Order Subnet Hosts needed Prefix (usable) Network Usable range Broadcast 1 Staff, VLAN 10 100 /25 (126) 172.16.0.0 .1 – .126 .127 2 Wireless, VLAN 30 50 /26 (62) 172.16.0.128 .129 – .190 .191 3 Printers/IoT, VLAN 40 20 /27 (30) 172.16.0.192 .193 – .222 .223 4 Management, VLAN 99 10 /28 (14) 172.16.0.224 .225 – .238 .239 5 R1–R2 link 2 /30 (2) 172.16.0.240 .241 – .242 .243 6 R1–R3 link 2 /30 (2) 172.16.0.244 .245 – .246 .247 — Spare — /29 172.16.0.248 .249 – .254 .255 Figure 2.4 draws this allocation to scale. Notice that the blocks never overlap and each one starts on a multiple of its own size. Allocating smallest-first often breaks that rule and wastes space. Figure 2.4 VLSM plan for 172.16.0.0/24, drawn to scale, with the last /27 enlarged The top bar of Figure 2.4 is the whole /24 from .0 to .255; the Staff /25 takes exactly half. The four smallest subnets share the last /27, which is enlarged underneath so their labels are readable. The dashed block is unallocated space for growth.

c: Chapter 2 · IPv4 addressing and subnetting
x: v2.0 does not name summarization as its own objective, but you need it to read routing tables (3.1) and to spot overlapping subnets. A summary route advertises several contiguous networks as one larger prefix. Method: write the octet that differs in binary, count the leading bits that are identical in all the networks, and add the bits of the octets before it. Example: 10.10.8.0/24, 10.10.9.0/24, 10.10.10.0/24, 10.10.11.0/24. The first two octets (16 bits) are identical. Third octets 8, 9, 10, 11 in binary: 00001000, 00001001, 00001010, 00001011. The first 6 bits match ( Figure 2.5 ). Summary prefix length = 16 + 6 = /22 . Network = the common bits followed by zeros = 10.10.8.0/22 (mask 255.255.252.0), covering 10.10.8.0 – 10.10.11.255. Figure 2.5 Summarizing 10.10.8.0/24 to 10.10.11.0/24 into 10.10.8.0/22 by comparing third-octet bits In Figure 2.5 the shaded third-octet bits are identical in all four networks; only the last two bits change (00, 01, 10, 11). Those two bits are exactly what four /24s need, so 22 bits name the whole group. Check: a /22 is a block of 4 in the third octet, and 8 is a multiple of 4, so the summary is exact. If the networks were 10.10.9.0 to 10.10.12.0, no single /22 would cover them without including extra space.

t: 3.3 Address format and the two compression rules
c: Chapter 3 · IPv6 addressing and prefix sizing
x: An IPv6 address is 128 bits written as 8 hextets (groups of 4 hexadecimal digits, 16 bits each) separated by colons. Hex digits are 0–9 and a–f; letters are case-insensitive, but lowercase is the recommended way to write them (RFC 5952). Full form: 2001:0db8:acad:0010:0000:0000:0000:0001 Rule 1 — drop leading zeros in each hextet: 0db8 → db8 , 0010 → 10 , 0000 → 0 . Never drop trailing zeros: acad stays acad , and 0010 is 10 , not 1 . Rule 2 — replace one run of consecutive all-zero hextets with :: , once per address: 2001:db8:acad:10:0:0:0:1 → 2001:db8:acad:10::1 . Full Shortest valid form Note 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329 Both rules fe80:0000:0000:0000:0250:79ff:fe66:6801 fe80::250:79ff:fe66:6801 Typical link-local 2001:0db8:0000:0001:0000:0000:0000:0001 2001:db8:0:1::1 :: goes on the longest zero run 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 ::1 Loopback 0000:...:0000 :: Unspecified address Invalid addresses the exam likes: 2001:db8::1::5 (two :: — the length becomes ambiguous); 2001:db8:g::1 ( g is not hex); 2001:db8:12345::1 (five digits in a hextet). Expanding back: count the hextets you can see, then fill the :: with enough 0000 groups to make 8. 2001:db8:a::12 shows 4 hextets, so :: = 4 zero hextets → 2001:0db8:000a:0000:0000:0000:0000:0012 .

IPv6 has no broadcast address and no "network and broadcast minus two" rule; every interface ID in the subnet is usable (the all-zeros ID is reserved as the subnet-router anycast address, which you rarely need to think about). A /48 holds 2^(64−48) = 2^16 = 65,536 /64s; a /56 holds 2^8 = 256 /64s; a /60 holds 16 . A readable plan for this guide. With the site prefix 2001:db8:acad::/48, the 4th hextet is the subnet ID. x: IPv6 has unicast (one interface), multicast (a group) and anycast (the nearest of several interfaces sharing an address). There is no broadcast; jobs that used broadcast in IPv4 (ARP, DHCP Discover) use multicast instead. Type Prefix / range Starts with Routed? What it is for Global unicast (GUA) 2000::/3 2 or 3 Yes, Internet-wide Public IPv6 addresses, like public IPv4 Link-local (LLA) fe80::/10 fe80 Never leaves the link Neighbor discovery, routing protocol neighbors, the default gateway address hosts use Unique local (ULA) fc00::/7 (in practice fd00::/8) fd Inside the organisation only Private addressing, similar in spirit to RFC 1918 (but not used with NAT) Loopback ::1/128 ::1 No Tests the host's own stack (like 127.0.0.1) Unspecified ::/128 :: No Source address before a host has one; ::/0 is the default route Multicast ff00::/8 ff Scope-dependent One-to-many delivery Every IPv6-enabled interface has a link-local address , even when it has no global address. That is why fe80:: addresses appear in ipconfig on almost every PC. Multicast addresses you must recognise (they make IPv6 work): Address Who listens ff02::1 All nodes on the link ff02::2 All routers on the link (joined after ipv6 unicast-routing ) ff02::5 / ff02::6 OSPFv3 routers / designated routers (Chapter 12) ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX Solicited-node multicast: the last 24 bits of a unicast address. t: 3.6 Modified EUI-64: building an interface ID from a MAC address
c: Chapter 3 · IPv6 addressing and prefix sizing
x: A 48-bit MAC address is too short for a 64-bit interface ID. Modified EUI-64 stretches it in three steps ( Figure 3.2 ). Worked example: PC1's MAC 0050.7966.6801 , subnet 2001:db8:acad:10::/64. Split the MAC in half: 0050.79 | 66.6801 . Insert FFFE in the middle: 0050:79ff:fe66:6801 . Flip the 7th bit of the first byte (the universal/local bit): first byte 00 = 00000000 → 00000010 = 02 . Interface ID: 0250:79ff:fe66:6801 . Add the prefix: global address 2001:db8:acad:10:250:79ff:fe66:6801 ; link-local fe80::250:79ff:fe66:6801 . Figure 3.2 Modified EUI-64 for MAC 0050.7966.6801: split, insert FFFE, flip the U/L bit Figure 3.2 follows the steps above byte by byte (each box is one byte, two hex digits). Highlighted boxes are the bytes that change at each step: FF FE is inserted in step 2, and only the first byte changes in step 3. Flipping, not setting. If the 7th bit is already 1 it becomes 0. MAC 0200.5e11.2233 : first byte 02 = 00000010 → 00000000 = 00 , giving interface ID 0000:5eff:fe11:2233 . On fe80::/64 that gives fe80::5eff:fe11:2233 ; on 2001:db8:acad:10::/64 it gives 2001:db8:acad:10:0:5eff:fe11:2233 . Quick hex trick for step 3: the 7th bit is worth 2 in the first byte, so add 2 if that bit is 0 (00→02, 0c→0e, a8→aa) or subtract 2 if it is 1 (02→00, 0e→0c). Only the second hex digit of the first byte ever changes. Who uses EUI-64? Cisco IOS uses it automatically for link-local addresses, and for global addresses when you add the eui-64 keyword. Modern Windows, macOS and Linux hosts usually generate random or stable-privacy interface IDs instead, so you cannot predict a PC's address from its MAC. The exam still expects you to calculate EUI-64 by hand. Memory trick EUI-64 in three moves: Split, Stuff, Flip — split the MAC in half, stuff FFFE in the middle, flip the 7th bit of the first byte.

t: 3.7 Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP): the engine behind IPv6
c: Chapter 3 · IPv6 addressing and prefix sizing
x: IPv6 has no ARP and no broadcast. NDP , carried in ICMPv6, does those jobs and more with five messages: Message ICMPv6 type Sent to Purpose Router Solicitation (RS) 133 ff02::2 (all routers) Host asks: "any routers here?" Router Advertisement (RA) 134 ff02::1 (all nodes), or the asking host Router announces prefix, prefix length, flags, and itself as a default gateway Neighbor Solicitation (NS) 135 Solicited-node multicast of the target "What is the MAC for this IPv6 address?" (replaces ARP request); also used for DAD Neighbor Advertisement (NA) 136 The asker (or ff02::1) "That address is mine; here is my MAC" (replaces ARP reply) Redirect 137 The host A better first hop exists on this link Duplicate Address Detection (DAD). Before using any unicast address, a node sends an NS for its own new address . If anyone answers with an NA, the address is a duplicate and is not used. A Cisco router logs %IPV6_ND-4-DUPLICATE , and Windows shows the address as "Duplicate". Because ICMPv6 carries NDP, blocking all ICMPv6 breaks IPv6. This matters later for ACLs.

c: Chapter 3 · IPv6 addressing and prefix sizing
x: IPv6 offers more ways to get an address than IPv4. What a host does is controlled by flags in the RA the router sends: A flag (Autonomous, in the prefix information): 1 = "build your own address from this prefix" (SLAAC). O flag (Other configuration): 1 = "ask a DHCPv6 server for other information" such as DNS servers. M flag (Managed): 1 = "get your address from a DHCPv6 server". Method RA flags Address comes from DNS comes from Default gateway comes from Static n/a Typed by hand Typed by hand Typed (or learned from RA) SLAAC only A=1, O=0, M=0 Host: prefix from RA + its own interface ID RA's DNS option (RDNSS), if sent RA (router's link-local) Stateless DHCPv6 (SLAAC + DHCPv6) A=1, O=1, M=0 Host via SLAAC Stateless DHCPv6 server RA Stateful DHCPv6 M=1 (A usually 0) DHCPv6 server DHCPv6 server RA — DHCPv6 never gives a gateway Exam tip The default gateway in IPv6 always comes from the Router Advertisement , never from DHCPv6. If routers stop sending RAs, hosts lose their gateway even with a working DHCPv6 server. Hosts normally use the router's link-local address (for example fe80::1 ) as their gateway.

PC1 sends a Router Solicitation to ff02::2 instead of waiting for the next periodic RA. RA. R1 replies with prefix 2001:db8:acad:10::/64, A=1, M=0, O=0, and a router lifetime that makes R1 (fe80::1) a default gateway. Build. PC1 combines the /64 prefix with an interface ID (EUI-64 or random) to form its global address. DAD again. PC1 sends an NS for its new global address. No NA comes back, so the address becomes valid. Ready. PC1 now has a link-local address, a global address and a default gateway, with no DHCP server involved. Figure 3.3 SLAAC message sequence between PC1 and R1, with DAD Read Figure 3.3 top to bottom; time runs downward and arrows show which device sends each NDP message. Steps 1 and 4 happen inside PC1 without any message to R1. The address built in step 4 is the EUI-64 result from Figure 3.2 ; a Windows PC would use a random interface ID instead. Why SLAAC needs /64: the host must add a 64-bit interface ID. If the RA advertises a /80 or /96 prefix, SLAAC hosts do not configure a global address.

c: Chapter 3 · IPv6 addressing and prefix sizing
x: 128 bits, 8 hextets. Drop leading zeros in each hextet; use :: once for the longest run of zero hextets. Structure: /48 site prefix + 16-bit subnet ID + 64-bit interface ID. Every LAN is /64 ; /127 for router links; /128 for loopbacks. /48 = 65,536 /64s; /56 = 256. Types: GUA 2000::/3; link-local fe80::/10 (every interface has one, never routed); ULA fc00::/7 (fd…); loopback ::1; unspecified ::; multicast ff00::/8. No broadcast. Key multicast: ff02::1 all nodes, ff02::2 all routers, ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX solicited-node (last 24 bits). EUI-64: split MAC, insert FFFE, flip the 7th bit (±2 on the first byte). Cisco uses it for link-local by default; modern PCs usually use random IDs. NDP (ICMPv6): RS 133, RA 134, NS 135, NA 136, Redirect 137. NS/NA replace ARP. DAD = NS for your own address. RA flags: A=1 SLAAC; O=1 stateless DHCPv6 for DNS; M=1 stateful DHCPv6. Gateway always from the RA. IOS: ipv6 unicast-routing (no RAs without it), ipv6 address x/64 , … eui-64 , ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local . Verify with show ipv6 interface brief , show ipv6 interface , show ipv6 route , show ipv6 neighbors . Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea " :: can be used twice to shorten more" Only once; twice makes the address ambiguous "0010 shortens to 1" Only leading zeros go: 0010 → 10 "IPv6 has broadcast like IPv4" No broadcast; multicast (ff02::1, solicited-node) does those jobs "DHCPv6 gives the default gateway" Gateway always comes from the Router Advertisement "EUI-64 sets the 7th bit to 1" It flips the bit: 1 becomes 0, 0 becomes 1 "Use /120 on a LAN to save space" LANs use /64; SLAAC breaks with longer prefixes

c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: A college lab server in Kathmandu might run a web server, a database, a DHCP server and a monitoring tool. Twenty years ago each would need its own physical machine, mostly sitting idle. Virtualization lets one physical server run many isolated workloads at once, each believing it has its own computer. The result is fewer servers, less power, faster deployment and easier recovery. For a network engineer, virtualization changes one thing above all: one switch port may now carry traffic for dozens of machines in several VLANs.

c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: Term Meaning Host The physical server (or laptop) that provides CPU, memory, storage and NICs Hypervisor Software that creates and runs VMs and shares the host's hardware among them (also called a virtual machine monitor) Virtual machine (VM) A complete software computer: virtual CPU (vCPU), memory, disk and NIC, running its own guest operating system Guest OS The OS inside a VM (Windows Server, Ubuntu, Cisco IOS XE in a virtual router) Virtual disk A file that acts as the VM's hard disk (.vmdk, .vhdx, .qcow2) Snapshot A saved point-in-time state you can roll back to Live migration Moving a running VM to another host without shutting it down (VMware vMotion, Hyper-V Live Migration) Container An isolated process (or group) that packages an application and its libraries but shares the host's OS kernel Image A read-only template from which VMs or containers are started Virtual switch (vSwitch) Software switch inside the host that connects VMs to each other and to the physical NICs

c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors run directly on the server hardware, with no general-purpose OS underneath. They are efficient and secure, and they run data centres. Examples: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, KVM (part of the Linux kernel), Xen. Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors run as an application on top of an ordinary OS. They are convenient for labs and desktops but add a layer of overhead. Examples: Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion, Parallels Desktop. Figure 4.1 compares the three software stacks, including containers. Figure 4.1 Software stacks: Type 1 hypervisor, Type 2 hypervisor and containers Read each column of Figure 4.1 from the hardware upward. A Type 1 hypervisor sits directly on the hardware; a Type 2 hypervisor needs a host OS beneath it. Containers drop the guest OS entirely, which is why they start in seconds and use far less memory. Type 1 (bare-metal) Type 2 (hosted) Runs on Hardware directly A host OS (Windows, macOS, Linux) Performance Near native Lower; host OS competes for resources Typical use Production servers, data centres, cloud Laptops, training labs, testing Examples ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, Xen VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels Management Central tools (vCenter, SCVMM) or web UI Desktop application Exam tip "bare-metal" always means Type 1; "runs on top of Windows/macOS" always means Type 2. Memory trick Type 1 sits 1st on the metal (bare-metal). Type 2 is the 2nd layer up — it runs on top of a host OS.

t: 4.5 How VMs connect to the network
c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: A VM has no physical cable. Its traffic travels through three pieces of software and then a physical NIC ( Figure 4.2 ): vNIC — the VM's virtual network card. It has its own MAC address, so the physical switch learns many MACs behind one port. Virtual switch (vSwitch) — a Layer 2 switch inside the hypervisor. It forwards frames between VMs on the same host without them ever reaching the physical network, and sends everything else out an uplink. Examples: VMware vSphere Standard and Distributed Switch, Hyper-V Virtual Switch, Linux bridge, Open vSwitch. Port group — a set of vSwitch ports sharing a policy, most importantly a VLAN ID . Put a VM's vNIC in the "Staff, VLAN 10" port group and its traffic belongs to VLAN 10. Uplinks (physical NICs) — the host's real NICs, for example vmnic0 and vmnic1. Because VMs in different VLANs share them, the uplinks normally carry an 802.1Q trunk to the physical switch. Two or more uplinks are often bundled (NIC teaming), which on the switch side may be an EtherChannel/LACP port channel. Figure 4.2 Virtual switching: vNICs, port groups, vSwitch and an LACP trunk to SW1 In Figure 4.2 arrows show outbound traffic. Each VM's vNIC sits in a port group, the vSwitch tags frames with that port group's VLAN, and the two highlighted uplinks carry the tagged frames to SW1 as one LACP bundle. SW1 must allow both VLANs on the trunk, or VMs in a missing VLAN are cut off. Step by step: VM-Web (VLAN 10) sends a packet to its gateway. VM-Web's vNIC sends an untagged frame into the Staff port group. The vSwitch knows the port group is VLAN 10, so it adds an 802.1Q tag with VLAN 10 when sending the frame out vmnic0. SW1 receives the tagged frame on its trunk and forwards it in VLAN 10 toward the gateway (an SVI or router). Replies come back tagged VLAN 10; the vSwitch removes the tag and delivers the frame to VM-Web. Recognising virtual MAC addresses. Hypervisors use their own OUIs, so a MAC table full of them tells you a port connects to a virtualization host: OUI (first 3 bytes) Usually means 00:50:56 VMware VM 00:15:5D Hyper-V VM 08:00:27 VirtualBox VM 52:54:00 KVM/QEMU VM SW1 Copy commands SW1# show mac address-table interface port-channel1 Mac Address Table ------------------------------------------- Vlan Mac Address Type Ports ---- ----------- -------- ----- 10 0050.56a1.0b01 DYNAMIC Po1 <- VM-Web 10 0050.56a1.0b02 DYNAMIC Po1 <- VM-DB 99 0050.56a1.0b03 DYNAMIC Po1 <- VM-Mgmt Three VMs in two VLANs, all learned on one logical port: exactly the picture in Figure 4.2 .

c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: A container packages one application with exactly the libraries it needs and runs it as an isolated process on a shared OS kernel. The Linux kernel features namespaces (each container sees its own processes, network interfaces and file system) and cgroups (limits on CPU and memory) provide the isolation. Term Meaning Image Read-only template: the app, its libraries and settings (for example nginx:latest ) Container A running instance of an image Registry Where images are stored and downloaded (Docker Hub, a private registry) Container engine / runtime Software that pulls images and runs containers (Docker, containerd, Podman) Orchestrator Runs many containers across many hosts, restarts failed ones, scales them (Kubernetes) How containers are networked ( Figure 4.3 ). By default Docker on Linux: Creates a Linux bridge called docker0 , normally 172.17.0.1/16. Gives each container a virtual interface on that bridge and an address such as 172.17.0.2. Uses NAT (masquerading) on the host so containers can reach outside networks using the host's IP. Makes a container reachable from outside only when a port is published : -p 8080:80 maps the host's port 8080 to the container's port 80. Figure 4.3 Default Docker networking: docker0 bridge, NAT and a published port (-p 8080:80) In Figure 4.3 the highlighted arrows trace a request from a laptop on the home LAN to the web container. Nothing outside the host can reach 172.17.0.2 directly; only the published port is exposed. This is the same NAT idea you will configure on routers in Chapter 21. Other modes exist: host networking (the container uses the host's interfaces directly), none (no network), and overlay networks that span several hosts in an orchestrated cluster.

Yes (Windows VM on a Linux host) Must match the host kernel type (Linux containers need a Linux kernel) Best for Different OSs, legacy apps, strong separation Microservices, fast scaling, CI/CD pipelines They are not rivals: in practice containers often run inside VMs , especially in the cloud.

c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: Network Functions Virtualization (NFV) runs network devices as software on standard servers instead of dedicated hardware. Examples from Cisco: Catalyst 8000V — a virtual IOS XE router (successor to the CSR 1000v), common in public clouds and data centres. Secure Firewall Threat Defense Virtual (FTDv) and ASAv — virtual firewalls. Virtual wireless controllers — controller software running as a VM (Chapter 7, objective 2.2.b). Lab tools use the same idea: Cisco Modeling Labs (CML) , GNS3 and EVE-NG run real IOS images as VMs or containers. Packet Tracer is different: it simulates device behaviour rather than running real Cisco software, which is why some features are missing (as noted in Part 0.4). Some Cisco switches and routers can also host containers themselves (Cisco IOx application hosting), but that is beyond the CCNA objectives.

t: 4.9 What virtualization means for the network engineer
c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: You rarely configure the hypervisor, but you configure the switch ports it plugs into, and you get the ticket when a VM "has no network". Three facts drive everything: One port, many MACs and VLANs. A host port is usually a trunk carrying every VLAN its VMs use. VMs move. Live migration can move a VM to another host at any moment, so every host in a cluster needs the same VLANs on its uplinks. The vSwitch and the physical switch must agree on VLAN IDs, the native VLAN, and how uplinks are bundled. A preview of the switch configuration (taught fully in Chapters 5–7): SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1 - 2 SW1(config-if-range)# description ESXi-01 vmnic0-1 SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,99 SW1(config-if-range)# switchport nonegotiate SW1(config-if-range)# spanning-tree portfast trunk SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active ! only if the host side uses LACP Notes: newer IOS releases write the PortFast command as spanning-tree portfast edge trunk . Bundle the ports with LACP only when the hypervisor's teaming is set to LACP (for example a VMware distributed switch with a LAG); many teaming modes expect two independent trunk ports instead. Troubleshooting virtualized hosts Symptom Likely cause What to check Fix VMs in one VLAN have no network; other VMs on the same host are fine VLAN not allowed on the trunk, or not created on the switch show interfaces trunk , show vlan brief Add the VLAN to the switch and the allowed list A VM sits in the wrong subnet Wrong VLAN ID on its port group Hypervisor port group settings; show mac address-table address <vm-mac> Correct the port group VLAN Intermittent loss; log shows %SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF NIC teaming and switch bundling disagree, so VM MACs flap between ports show logging , show etherchannel summary Make teaming and switch configuration match (both LACP, or both independent) VM loses network after live migration Destination host's uplinks lack that VLAN Compare trunks on all hosts in the cluster Make trunks identical across the cluster Two VMs fight over an address after cloning Clone kept the same static IP or MAC show ip arp , duplicate-address warnings Regenerate the MAC, re-address the clone Native VLAN mismatch messages vSwitch untagged traffic and switch native VLAN differ CDP log %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH Align native VLANs (or tag everything) Container works from the host, not from the LAN Port not published, or host firewall blocks it docker ps (PORTS column) Publish with -p , open the firewall

t: 4.10 Hands-on Lab 4.1 — VMs and containers on your own laptop (Beginner)
c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: Objective: 1.2. PT note: Packet Tracer cannot run VMs or containers, so this lab uses free tools on your laptop. It is optional for the exam but makes every concept in this chapter concrete. You need: Oracle VirtualBox (free), an Ubuntu Server ISO, about 20 GB of disk and 2 GB of spare RAM. Your laptop is the host; VirtualBox is a Type 2 hypervisor. Figure 4.4 shows the three VirtualBox network modes you will test. Figure 4.4 VirtualBox NAT, Bridged and Host-only modes with example addresses In Figure 4.4 the highlighted line is the VM's path. In NAT mode it hides behind the host; in Bridged mode it connects to the home router as if it were a separate PC; in Host-only mode it can reach only the host. The addresses are VirtualBox defaults and a typical home network; yours may differ. Part A — Build the VM In VirtualBox create a VM: Linux / Ubuntu (64-bit), 2 vCPU, 2048 MB RAM, 20 GB virtual disk. Install Ubuntu Server from the ISO, accepting the defaults. Log in and run ip link show . The interface (usually enp0s3 ) has a MAC starting 08:00:27 — the VirtualBox OUI from 4.5. Part B — NAT mode (the default) terminal Copy commands $ ip -4 addr show enp0s3 inet 10.0.2.15/24 ... dynamic enp0s3 $ ip route default via 10.0.2.2 dev enp0s3 ... $ ping -c 2 1.1.1.1 # works if your laptop has Internet From the laptop, try ping 10.0.2.15 : it fails. The VM is hidden behind VirtualBox's NAT, just like a home PC behind a router. Part C — Bridged mode Power off the VM. In Settings → Network → Adapter 1 choose Bridged Adapter and select the laptop's Wi-Fi or Ethernet card. Start the VM and run ip -4 addr show enp0s3 . It now has an address from your home router (for example 192.168.1.60). From the laptop, ping that address: it succeeds. The VM is a full member of your LAN. If it gets no address, some Wi-Fi and campus networks block extra MAC addresses on one connection; use Ethernet or Host-only mode instead. Part D — Host-only mode In File → Tools → Network Manager confirm a host-only network exists (by default 192.168.56.1/24 with DHCP). Set Adapter 1 to Host-only Adapter and restart the VM. It receives an address such as 192.168.56.101. The laptop can ping it, but the VM has no Internet. Add a second adapter in NAT mode if it needs updates. Part E — Containers inside the VM (use Bridged mode so you can browse to it) terminal Copy commands $ sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y docker.io $ sudo docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx $ ip -4 addr show docker0 inet 172.17.0.1/16 ... docker0 $ sudo docker inspect -f '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' web 172.17.0.2 $ sudo docker port web 80/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:8080 Now open http://<VM address>:8080 in your laptop's browser: the nginx welcome page appears. You have just reproduced Figure 4.3 — a container on the docker0 bridge, reachable only through the published port. Your VM is the Docker host. Troubleshooting Problem Cause Fix Bridged VM gets no IP Network blocks extra MACs, or wrong host adapter selected Choose the correct adapter; use Ethernet or Host-only permission denied on docker commands User is not in the docker group Use sudo , or sudo usermod -aG docker $USER and log in again Browser cannot reach port 8080 VM in NAT mode, or container not running Use Bridged mode; check sudo docker ps docker run cannot download nginx VM has no Internet (Host-only mode) Add a NAT adapter or switch to Bridged Questions to answer Why could the laptop not ping the VM in NAT mode? Which mode makes the VM look like a separate physical PC to your home router? Which address does the outside world use to reach the nginx container: 172.17.0.2 or the VM's address? Why? c: Chapter 4 · Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers
x: Hypervisor = software that runs VMs and shares hardware among them. Type 1 runs on bare metal (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, Xen); Type 2 runs on a host OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels). VM = full computer in software with its own guest OS : strong isolation, gigabytes, slower to start, can run a different OS. Container = app + libraries sharing the host kernel : megabytes, starts in about a second, weaker isolation. Image → container; registry stores images; Docker/containerd run them; Kubernetes orchestrates them. VM networking: vNIC (own MAC) → port group (VLAN ID) → vSwitch (adds 802.1Q tag) → physical NIC uplinks → trunk (often an LACP bundle) to the physical switch. Container networking: docker0 bridge (172.17.0.0/16 by default), NAT outbound, published ports ( -p host:container ) inbound. NFV: virtual routers and firewalls (Catalyst 8000V, FTDv, ASAv) and virtual WLCs run as VMs. Virtual OUIs: 00:50:56 VMware, 00:15:5D Hyper-V, 08:00:27 VirtualBox, 52:54:00 KVM. Network impact: trunks must allow every VM VLAN on every host in the cluster; teaming and switch bundling must match; clones can duplicate IPs. Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea "Containers are small VMs" Containers have no guest OS; they share the host's kernel "Type 2 means a second-generation hypervisor" Type 2 means hosted on an OS; Type 1 means bare metal "A host port should be an access port in the main server VLAN" It is usually a trunk carrying every VLAN its VMs use "VMs on the same host always talk through the physical switch" VMs in the same VLAN on one host talk through the vSwitch without leaving the host

c: Chapter 5 · VLANs, trunks, Layer 2/Layer 3 interfaces and SVIs
x: Without VLANs, every device on a switch shares one broadcast domain. In a 300-user college building, every ARP request and DHCP Discover reaches every PC, printer and phone; a guest laptop sits on the same network as the accounts office. VLANs (virtual LANs) let you group ports logically — Staff, Wireless, Printers, Management — regardless of which switch they are on, and keep each group's broadcasts and traffic separate. Moving traffic between VLANs then requires a router or Layer 3 switch, which is where security policy can be applied.

c: Chapter 5 · VLANs, trunks, Layer 2/Layer 3 interfaces and SVIs
x: A VLAN is a broadcast domain ( Figure 5.1 ). A switch forwards a frame only to ports in the same VLAN. Each VLAN normally maps to one IP subnet; this guide uses 10.10. VLAN .0/24. Figure 5.1 Three VLANs on one switch: a broadcast stays inside its own VLAN In Figure 5.1 the dashed boxes are VLAN memberships, not separate hardware. The arrows trace PC1's broadcast: SW1 floods it only to PC2, the one other port in VLAN 10. PC3, PC4 and the printer never see it, even though they are on the same switch. VLAN range Use 1 Default VLAN: every port starts in it; cannot be deleted. Also the default native VLAN 2–1001 Normal range: user VLANs 1002–1005 Reserved for legacy Token Ring and FDDI; cannot be deleted 1006–4094 Extended range (needs VTP transparent mode or VTPv3 on older switches) 0 and 4095 Reserved, never used Benefits: smaller broadcast domains, security separation (a firewall or ACL controls inter-VLAN traffic), logical grouping across buildings, and easier management (move a user by changing one port). Best practices used in this guide: Do not put users in VLAN 1. Use a dedicated management VLAN (99). Use an unused VLAN as the trunk native VLAN (999), not VLAN 1. Shut down unused ports and put them in an unused "parking" VLAN. Allow only the VLANs you need on each trunk. About VTP. VLAN Trunking Protocol can copy VLAN lists between switches, but it is not a v2.0 objective and a mistake can delete VLANs network-wide. This guide creates VLANs on each switch by hand (VTP transparent or off).

t: 5.4 Creating VLANs and Layer 2 access ports (2.1.a)
c: Chapter 5 · VLANs, trunks, Layer 2/Layer 3 interfaces and SVIs
x: A Layer 2 interface (a switchport ) forwards frames by MAC address within a VLAN. An access port belongs to exactly one data VLAN and sends and receives untagged frames; it connects end devices. Step 1 — create and name the VLANs (global configuration, then VLAN configuration mode): SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# vlan 10 SW1(config-vlan)# name STAFF SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 30 SW1(config-vlan)# name WIRELESS SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 40 SW1(config-vlan)# name PRINTERS SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 99 SW1(config-vlan)# name MGMT SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 999 SW1(config-vlan)# name NATIVE SW1(config-vlan)# exit Step 2 — make the port an access port and assign the VLAN: SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1 SW1(config-if)# description PC1 - Staff SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10 SW1(config-if)# exit SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/3 - 24 SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown ! unused ports off Command Mode Purpose Notes and common mistakes vlan <id> Global config Creates the VLAN and enters VLAN config mode Assigning a port to a VLAN that does not exist creates it automatically on most switches, but naming it is still good practice name <text> VLAN config Names the VLAN Names are local labels; they do not need to match between switches (but should) switchport mode access Interface config Forces access mode and disables trunk negotiation (DTP) Leaving the default dynamic mode can accidentally form a trunk switchport access vlan <id> Interface config Puts the port in that VLAN Applies only while the port is in access mode interface range fa0/3 - 24 Global config Configures many ports at once Spaces around the hyphen are required on some IOS versions no vlan <id> Global config Deletes a VLAN Ports assigned to it stay assigned but become inactive and pass no traffic until the VLAN is recreated Verification: SW1 Copy commands SW1# show vlan brief VLAN Name Status Ports ---- -------------------------------- --------- ------------------------------ 1 default active Fa0/3, Fa0/4, Fa0/5, Fa0/6 ... 10 STAFF active Fa0/1 30 WIRELESS active Fa0/2 40 PRINTERS active 99 MGMT active 999 NATIVE active 1002 fddi-default act/unsup ... Exam tip Trunk ports do not appear in show vlan brief ; only access ports are listed. A port "missing" from every VLAN is probably a trunk. SW1 Copy commands SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/1 switchport Name: Fa0/1 Switchport: Enabled Administrative Mode: static access Operational Mode: static access Access Mode VLAN: 10 (STAFF) Trunking Native Mode VLAN: 1 (default) Voice VLAN: none ... Administrative Mode is what you configured; Operational Mode is what the port is actually doing. When they differ, negotiation (DTP) or an error is involved.

c: Chapter 5 · VLANs, trunks, Layer 2/Layer 3 interfaces and SVIs
x: When VLAN 10 exists on two switches, the link between them must carry VLAN 10 — and VLAN 30, 40 and 99 too. Rather than one cable per VLAN, a trunk carries many VLANs over one link by tagging each frame with its VLAN ID. IEEE 802.1Q is the standard (Cisco's old ISL is obsolete). The 802.1Q tag ( Figure 5.2 ). The sending switch inserts 4 bytes between the source MAC and the Type field: Figure 5.2 802.1Q tag position in the Ethernet frame and its four fields Figure 5.2 zooms into the highlighted tag from Figure 1.3 's frame. The 12-bit VID is what tells the receiving switch which VLAN the frame belongs to; the 3-bit PCP is reused for voice priority in Chapter 7. Field Size Meaning TPID 16 bits Always 0x8100: "this frame is tagged" PCP 3 bits Priority (Class of Service) 0–7; IP phones use 5 for voice DEI 1 bit Drop eligible indicator (formerly CFI) VID 12 bits VLAN ID: 1–4094 usable Because the frame changes, the switch recalculates the FCS. The maximum frame size grows from 1518 to 1522 bytes. How a frame crosses a trunk ( Figure 5.3 ): PC1 sends an ordinary, untagged frame into its access port on SW1 (VLAN 10). SW1 decides the destination is reachable through the trunk Gi0/1 and inserts an 802.1Q tag with VID 10. SW2 receives the tagged frame, reads VID 10, and forwards it only to VLAN 10 ports. SW2 removes the tag before sending the frame out the access port to PC3, which never sees a tag. Figure 5.3 A VLAN 10 frame crossing an 802.1Q trunk between SW1 and SW2 Figure 5.3 matches the four steps above. Arrows show the direction of travel; the thick highlighted link is the trunk. The tag exists only on the trunk, which is why end devices on access ports never need to know VLANs exist. The native VLAN. Frames in the trunk's native VLAN cross the link untagged , and untagged frames received on a trunk are placed in the native VLAN. The default is VLAN 1. Both ends must use the same native VLAN; otherwise traffic leaks between VLANs and CDP reports %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH . Best practice: set it to an unused VLAN (999) on both ends. Configuring a trunk: SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1 SW1(config-if)# description Trunk to DSW1 Gi1/0/1 SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q ! only on switches that also support ISL SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999 SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,30,40,99 SW1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate ! stop sending DTP Command Purpose Notes and common mistakes switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q Chooses 802.1Q Needed only on platforms that support ISL (for example Catalyst 3560); if switchport mode trunk is rejected with "encapsulation is Auto", add this first. Catalyst 2960 and many newer switches support only 802.1Q and do not have the command switchport mode trunk Forces trunking Both ends should be configured as trunks switchport trunk native vlan 999 Sets the untagged VLAN Must match on both ends switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,30,40,99 Replaces the allowed list Typing allowed vlan 50 later replaces the list with only 50 switchport trunk allowed vlan add 50 Adds one VLAN to the list The safe way to add; also remove 50 , except 50 , all , none switchport nonegotiate Disables DTP frames Use on manually configured trunks and access ports DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol). A Cisco-proprietary protocol that lets ports negotiate trunking. Its modes and the result for each pair: Side A \ Side B access trunk dynamic desirable dynamic auto access Access Mismatch (do not do this) Access Access trunk Mismatch Trunk Trunk Trunk dynamic desirable Access Trunk Trunk Trunk dynamic auto Access Trunk Trunk Access The classic exam trap: two ports left at dynamic auto (a common default) both wait to be asked and never form a trunk. Best practice is to hard-code switchport mode trunk or switchport mode access and disable DTP, because an attacker's PC can otherwise negotiate a trunk (VLAN hopping). Memory tric

t: 5.6 Layer 3 routed ports on a switch (2.1.a)
c: Chapter 5 · VLANs, trunks, Layer 2/Layer 3 interfaces and SVIs
x: A multilayer (Layer 3) switch such as a Catalyst 3650 or 9300 can also route. Any physical port can be turned into a routed port : it stops being a switchport, belongs to no VLAN, and takes an IP address like a router interface. Routed ports are used for switch-to-router and switch-to-switch links in routed campus designs. DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# ip routing ! enable IPv4 routing on the switch DSW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/24 DSW1(config-if)# description Routed link to R1 G0/0/0 DSW1(config-if)# no switchport ! Layer 2 -> Layer 3 DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.0.2 255.255.255.252 DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown Layer 2 switchport Layer 3 routed port Command switchport (default on Catalyst switches) no switchport Belongs to A VLAN (access) or many VLANs (trunk) No VLAN Addressing None on the port IP address on the port Typical link To end devices, to other switches To a router, or between Layer 3 switches Spanning tree Participates Does not run STP on that port ip routing is off by default on many Layer 3 switches. Without it, SVIs and routed ports still get addresses, but the switch will not route between them — a very common lab fault.

t: 5.7 Switch virtual interfaces and inter-VLAN routing (2.1.d)
c: Chapter 5 · VLANs, trunks, Layer 2/Layer 3 interfaces and SVIs
x: A switch virtual interface (SVI) is a logical Layer 3 interface for a VLAN: interface vlan 10 . It gives the switch an IP address inside that VLAN. SVIs have two uses. 1. Management SVI on a Layer 2 switch. An access switch needs one IP address so you can reach it with SSH, SNMP and syslog: SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# interface vlan 99 SW1(config-if)# description Management SW1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.99.11 255.255.255.0 SW1(config-if)# no shutdown SW1(config-if)# exit SW1(config)# ip default-gateway 10.10.99.1 ! a Layer 2 switch is a host: it needs a gateway 2. Gateway SVIs on a multilayer switch (inter-VLAN routing). Each VLAN's SVI is the default gateway for that VLAN, and the switch routes between SVIs internally: DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# ip routing DSW1(config)# interface vlan 10 DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0 DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown DSW1(config-if)# interface vlan 30 DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.30.1 255.255.255.0 DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown When is an SVI up/up? All of these must be true: The VLAN exists in the switch's VLAN database and is active. At least one port in that VLAN (an access port, or a trunk allowing it) is up and in the STP forwarding state. The SVI is not administratively shut down ( no shutdown ; SVIs start shut on many switches). This "autostate" behaviour is why an SVI shows up/down when its VLAN has no active ports. Comparing inter-VLAN routing methods ( Figure 5.4 ). Figure 5.4 Inter-VLAN routing: router-on-a-stick (left) vs multilayer switch SVIs (right) The highlighted arrows in Figure 5.4 trace a packet from a VLAN 10 host to a VLAN 30 host. On the left it travels up the trunk to R1 in VLAN 10 and comes back down the same trunk in VLAN 30. On the right it is routed between the two SVIs inside DSW1 and never leaves the switch. Method How Pros Cons Router-on-a-stick One router interface, one 802.1Q subinterface per VLAN, trunk to the switch Cheap; works with a Layer 2 switch Single link carries traffic twice (hairpin); router CPU and link become bottlenecks Multilayer switch SVIs One SVI per VLAN, ip routing Hardware speed, scales, no extra link Needs a Layer 3 switch Separate router interface per VLAN (legacy) One physical router port per VLAN, access links Simple Wastes ports; does not scale Router-on-a-stick configuration (the switch side is a normal trunk): R1 Copy commands R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/1 R1(config-if)# no shutdown ! enable the physical interface R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/1.10 R1(config-subif)# description Gateway VLAN 10 R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 10 R1(config-subif)# ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0 R1(config-subif)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/1.30 R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 30 R1(config-subif)# ip address 10.10.30.1 255.255.255.0 R1(config-subif)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/1.999 R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 999 native ! match the switch's native VLAN The subinterface number (.10) is only a label; the encapsulation dot1Q 10 command is what ties it to VLAN 10. Making them match is good practice. Packet walk: PC1 (VLAN 10) to PC2 (VLAN 30) through DSW1 SVIs. PC1 sees 10.10.30.11 is in another subnet, so it ARPs for its gateway 10.10.10.1 and sends the frame to the VLAN 10 SVI's MAC. The frame arrives on DSW1 in VLAN 10 (tagged on the trunk from SW1, or untagged on an access port). DSW1 routes the packet: destination 10.10.30.0/24 is connected via Vlan30 . DSW1 ARPs for PC2 in VLAN 30 if needed, builds a new frame, and sends it out the VLAN 30 port or trunk. PC2 receives it from the SVI's MAC as the source. The IP addresses never changed; the MAC addresses did (Chapter 1, Figure 1.2 ).

c: Chapter 5 · VLANs, trunks, Layer 2/Layer 3 interfaces and SVIs
x: VLAN = broadcast domain = (usually) one subnet. Ranges: 1 default; 2–1001 normal; 1002–1005 reserved; 1006–4094 extended. Access port: switchport mode access , switchport access vlan <id> ; untagged; one VLAN. Deleting a VLAN leaves its ports inactive . Trunk: switchport mode trunk (+ switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q on ISL-capable switches), native vlan , allowed vlan — use add to append. 802.1Q tag = 4 bytes: TPID 0x8100, PCP 3 bits, DEI 1 bit, VID 12 bits . Native VLAN: untagged on the trunk; must match both ends; default VLAN 1; best practice an unused VLAN. DTP: auto + auto = access; desirable + auto/desirable/trunk = trunk. Hard-code modes and use switchport nonegotiate . show vlan brief lists access ports only; trunks appear in show interfaces trunk (allowed → active → forwarding). Routed port: no switchport + ip address ; no VLAN, no STP. Multilayer switches need ip routing . SVI: interface vlan <id> ; up/up only if the VLAN exists, has an active forwarding port, and the SVI is no shutdown . Layer 2 switches need ip default-gateway for their management SVI. Router-on-a-stick: subinterface + encapsulation dot1Q <vlan> (+ native for the native VLAN); the physical interface must be no shutdown . Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea " allowed vlan 50 adds VLAN 50" It replaces the list; use allowed vlan add 50 "A trunk port is missing from show vlan brief , so it is broken" Trunks are never listed there "The subinterface number sets the VLAN" encapsulation dot1Q <id> sets it "An SVI with an IP is always up" It needs an active, forwarding port in its VLAN "A Layer 3 switch routes by default" Many need ip routing first

t: 6.2 Introduction: two cables are not automatically twice the bandwidth
c: Chapter 6 · EtherChannel with LACP
x: In Lab 5.1, SW1 has one 1 Gb/s uplink to DSW1. If you add a second cable for more bandwidth and redundancy, Spanning Tree Protocol (Chapter 9) sees a loop and blocks one of the links ( Figure 6.1 , left). You pay for two links but use one. EtherChannel bundles up to eight parallel physical links into one logical link called a port-channel (Po). STP, the MAC table and routing all see a single interface, so every member forwards traffic ( Figure 6.1 , right). If a member fails, traffic shifts to the survivors in well under a second without any STP recalculation. Figure 6.1 Two parallel links with STP (left) vs the same links bundled as EtherChannel Po1 (right) In Figure 6.1 the cabling is identical on both sides; only the configuration differs. On the left, STP must block the red dashed link to prevent a loop. On the right, the ellipse marks the bundle: STP treats Po1 as one port, so both highlighted links carry traffic.

c: Chapter 6 · EtherChannel with LACP
x: You add physical ports to a channel group with channel-group <n> mode <mode> . The switch creates interface port-channel \ , the logical interface you configure and monitor. A negotiation protocol (LACP or PAgP) checks that the far end agrees and that the members are compatible. Compatible members become bundled ; the port-channel comes up. Each frame is assigned to one member by a hash of its addresses (6.4), so one conversation always uses one link. Term Meaning EtherChannel Cisco's name for link aggregation Port-channel (Po) The logical interface representing the bundle Member (bundled) port A physical interface inside the bundle Channel group The number that ties members to their port-channel (Po1 = group 1) LACP Link Aggregation Control Protocol, IEEE 802.3ad (now 802.1AX), open standard PAgP Port Aggregation Protocol, Cisco proprietary (recognise it; v2.0 names only LACP)

t: 6.4 Load balancing: per flow, not per packet
c: Chapter 6 · EtherChannel with LACP
x: EtherChannel does not split one transfer across all links. The switch runs a hash on fields of each frame — source and/or destination MAC, IP address or port — and the result picks one member. Every frame of the same flow produces the same hash, so it always uses the same link and arrives in order ( Figure 6.2 ). Figure 6.2 Per-flow load balancing across the two members of Po1 In Figure 6.2 the highlighted flows hash to member Gi0/1 and the grey flows to Gi0/2. Which flow lands on which link depends on the hash result, not on the order the flows started. One large file copy between two hosts is limited to one member's speed (1 Gb/s on a 2 × 1 Gb/s bundle). Many flows between many hosts spread across all members. If traffic is uneven, choose a hash with more variety. Between Layer 3 devices, src-dst-ip usually spreads better than src-mac (all routed frames share the router's MAC). DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip ! global; applies to all bundles DSW1# show etherchannel load-balance EtherChannel Load-Balancing Configuration: src-dst-ip The default method and the available options vary by platform. Each end chooses its own method independently; they do not have to match.

c: Chapter 6 · EtherChannel with LACP
x: Mode Protocol Behaviour active LACP Sends LACP packets and starts negotiation passive LACP Answers LACP but never starts it desirable PAgP Sends PAgP and starts negotiation auto PAgP Answers PAgP but never starts it on None Bundles unconditionally, no negotiation Which pairs form a bundle? Side A \ Side B active passive on desirable / auto active Yes Yes No No (different protocols) passive Yes No — both wait No No on No No Yes No The same logic applies to PAgP: desirable + desirable or desirable + auto bundle; auto + auto does not. Best practice Use LACP active on both ends. It is an open standard (works with servers, hypervisors and other vendors), detects mis-cabling, and removes a member that stops talking LACP. Avoid on : if one end bundles and the other does not, you can create a forwarding loop. LACP details worth knowing: LACP can manage up to 16 links per bundle, of which 8 are active and up to 8 are hot-standby. Each side has a system priority (lower wins and decides which links are active) and each port a port priority ; defaults are 32768. Memory trick LACP: A ctive a sks, P assive p auses. PAgP: D esirable asks, A uto waits. Two that only wait (passive + passive, auto + auto) never form a channel.

x: EtherChannel bundles up to 8 active links into one logical port-channel ; STP, MAC learning and routing see one interface. LACP can hold 8 more in hot-standby (16 total). Load balancing is per flow (hash of MAC/IP/port). One flow never exceeds one member's speed. port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip is a common choice. Modes: LACP active / passive ; PAgP desirable / auto ; static on . passive + passive and auto + auto never bundle; protocols cannot mix; on bundles only with on . Best practice: LACP active on both ends. Members must match: speed, duplex, switchport type, mode, access VLAN or native + allowed VLANs. Layer 2 Po: channel-group n mode active on members, then configure interface port-channel n (trunk settings are copied to members). Layer 3 Po: no switchport on members before channel-group ; IP address on the port-channel. Verify: show etherchannel summary — Po(SU) Layer 2 in use, Po(RU) Layer 3 in use; members (P) bundled, (I) stand-alone, (s) suspended, (D) down. Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea "A 2 × 1 Gb/s bundle gives one download 2 Gb/s" One flow uses one member: 1 Gb/s "passive on both ends is the safe choice" Neither side starts LACP; no bundle forms "Put the IP address on each member of a Layer 3 bundle" One IP, on the port-channel interface "Channel-group numbers must match on both switches" They are local; matching is only good documentation "Fix a suspended member by changing that member" Configure the port-channel so all members inherit identical settings
