c: Chapter 7 · Edge-host ports: VLAN, PoE, port channel and LACP
x: PoE delivers DC power over the same twisted-pair cable as data, so phones, APs, cameras and IoT sensors need no power socket. The switch is the PSE (power sourcing equipment); the device is the PD (powered device). How a PoE port powers a device: Detection — the switch applies a low test voltage and looks for a PD's signature resistance. A PC NIC has none, so it never receives power. Classification — the PD signals a power class (and with LLDP-MED or CDP can negotiate a more exact amount). Power-up — if the switch's remaining power budget covers the request, it supplies power; otherwise it denies power and logs it. Monitoring — if the PD is unplugged or draws too much, power is removed. Standard Common name Power at the switch port Typical devices IEEE 802.3af (Type 1) PoE 15.4 W IP phones, basic cameras IEEE 802.3at (Type 2) PoE+ 30 W Most Wi-Fi 5/6 APs, PTZ cameras IEEE 802.3bt Type 3 PoE++ / 4-pair 60 W High-end APs, video phones IEEE 802.3bt Type 4 PoE++ 90 W Displays, small switches The device receives slightly less than the switch sends (cable loss). Cisco's UPOE and UPOE+ are proprietary equivalents at 60 W and 90 W. Configuration (interface mode; most PoE switches default to auto ): Command Effect power inline auto Detect and power any PD up to the port's maximum (default) power inline auto max 15400 Same, but cap the port at 15.4 W (value in milliwatts) power inline static max 30000 Reserve 30 W for this port in advance, even before a device connects power inline never Disable PoE on the port Verification (example output; columns and values vary by platform): SW4 Copy commands SW4# show power inline Module Available Used Remaining (Watts) (Watts) (Watts) ------ --------- -------- --------- 1 390.0 21.7 368.3 Interface Admin Oper Power Device Class Max (Watts) --------- ------ ---------- ------- ------------------- ----- ---- Gi1/0/1 auto off 0.0 n/a n/a 30.0 Gi1/0/2 auto on 6.3 IP Phone 7960 2 30.0 Gi1/0/3 off off 0.0 n/a n/a 30.0 Gi1/0/4 auto on 15.4 AIR-AP 3 30.0 Read it as: the switch has 390 W of PoE budget, 21.7 W is in use; the phone on Gi1/0/2 and the AP on Gi1/0/4 are powered; Gi1/0/1 has a PC (no PD detected, so off ); Gi1/0/3 was set to never (Admin off ). PoE troubleshooting: a device with no lights on a PoE port means check (1) the port is not never , (2) the switch's remaining budget, (3) the device's class against the port's maximum (an AP needing PoE+ on a PoE-only port may boot with reduced radios or not at all), (4) the cable. A state of faulty or err-disable usually means overcurrent or a bad cable or device. Memory trick PoE standards go alphabetically up in power: af (PoE, 15.4 W) → at (PoE+, 30 W) → bt (PoE++, 60 W and up).

t: 7.5 IP phones and the voice VLAN (2.2.c)
c: Chapter 7 · Edge-host ports: VLAN, PoE, port channel and LACP
x: Offices save cabling by plugging the PC into the back of the IP phone, so one switch port serves two devices in two VLANs : the phone in the voice VLAN and the PC in the data VLAN. Separating voice lets you give it priority (QoS) and keep it away from user traffic. How it works ( Figure 7.2 ): Figure 7.2 IP phone and PC sharing one switch port: voice VLAN 20 tagged, data VLAN 10 untagged In Figure 7.2 the dashed arrow is the CDP or LLDP-MED message that tells the phone its voice VLAN. The highlighted link between switch and phone carries both kinds of frame shown in the cards beneath it, and it also carries PoE power. Only untagged data crosses the phone-to-PC link. The switch powers the phone with PoE . The switch tells the phone its voice VLAN using CDP (Cisco phones) or LLDP-MED (other vendors): "use VLAN 20 for voice". The phone contains a small three-port switch : one port to the wall, one for the PC, one internal for the phone itself. The phone sends its own traffic tagged with VLAN 20 and CoS 5 (the 802.1Q PCP field from Figure 5.2 ). The PC's frames pass through the phone untagged , and the switch places them in the access VLAN 10. The phone gets its IP address by DHCP in the voice subnet (10.10.20.0/24 in this guide). Configuration: SW4 Copy commands SW4(config)# vlan 20 SW4(config-vlan)# name VOICE SW4(config-vlan)# exit SW4(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/2 SW4(config-if)# description IP phone + PC-B SW4(config-if)# switchport mode access SW4(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10 ! data VLAN for the PC SW4(config-if)# switchport voice vlan 20 ! voice VLAN for the phone SW4(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast SW4(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable SW4(config-if)# power inline auto Verification: SW4 Copy commands SW4# show interfaces gigabitethernet1/0/2 switchport Name: Gi1/0/2 Switchport: Enabled Administrative Mode: static access Operational Mode: static access Access Mode VLAN: 10 (STAFF) Voice VLAN: 20 (VOICE) ... SW4# show cdp neighbors Device ID Local Intrfce Holdtme Capability Platform Port ID SEP0001C7A1B2C3 Gig 1/0/2 150 H P M IP Phone Port 1 Exam points: The port is still an access port ( static access ); it is not a trunk and does not appear in show interfaces trunk , even though voice frames are tagged. The voice VLAN must exist on the switch and be carried on the uplink trunks ( allowed vlan add 20 ). Older Cisco documentation called this an "auxiliary VLAN". QoS trust settings for voice (for example mls qos trust device cisco-phone on some platforms) are beyond the v2.0 objectives. Troubleshooting phones: phone dark → PoE (7.4); phone gets an address in the data subnet → voice VLAN missing on the port, or CDP/LLDP disabled so the phone never learned VLAN 20; phone works but PC does not → access VLAN wrong; both fail beyond the switch → VLAN 20 or 10 not allowed on the uplink trunk.

x: An AP bridges Wi-Fi clients onto the wired network. Each SSID (wireless network name) maps to a VLAN — for example Staff-WiFi to VLAN 30 and Guest to VLAN 35. Where that mapping happens decides how the switch port is configured ( Figure 7.3 ). Figure 7.3 Standalone AP on a trunk (left) vs controller-based AP on an access port with a CAPWAP tunnel (right) On the left of Figure 7.3 the AP itself maps each SSID to a VLAN, so its port must carry all of them as a trunk. On the right the dashed CAPWAP tunnel carries client traffic from the AP across the switched network to the WLC, which maps SSIDs to VLANs on its own trunk; the AP's port needs only VLAN 99. Standalone (autonomous) AP. The AP is configured individually and bridges each SSID straight onto its VLAN. Its switch port must therefore be a trunk : the AP's own management address is usually in the native VLAN (untagged), and each SSID's VLAN is tagged. SW4 Copy commands SW4(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/4 SW4(config-if)# description AP-Lobby (standalone) SW4(config-if)# switchport mode trunk SW4(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99 ! AP management, untagged SW4(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 30,35,99 SW4(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk SW4(config-if)# power inline auto Controller-based (lightweight) AP in local mode. The AP is managed by a wireless LAN controller (WLC) . It builds a CAPWAP tunnel to the WLC — control on UDP 5246 (encrypted with DTLS) and data on UDP 5247 — and sends every client frame inside that tunnel. The WLC places client traffic on the right VLAN. The AP's switch port therefore needs only the AP management VLAN , as an access port: SW4 Copy commands SW4(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/5 SW4(config-if)# description LAP-1 (controller-based, local mode) SW4(config-if)# switchport mode access SW4(config-if)# switchport access vlan 99 SW4(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast SW4(config-if)# power inline auto The WLC's own uplink is a trunk carrying the client VLANs (30, 35) and its management VLAN, often bundled for redundancy. Older AireOS controllers bundle with static mode on (no LACP), while Catalyst 9800 controllers support LACP — check the platform before choosing the channel mode. AP type Switch port Why Standalone (autonomous) Trunk; native = AP management; SSID VLANs tagged The AP itself puts each SSID on its VLAN Controller-based, local mode Access in the AP management VLAN Client traffic is tunnelled to the WLC Controller-based, FlexConnect (local switching) Trunk, like standalone The AP switches client traffic locally at a branch Cloud-managed (for example Meraki) Usually trunk Managed from the cloud; traffic is bridged locally How a lightweight AP joins a WLC (step by step): the AP boots on PoE → gets an IP address by DHCP in VLAN 99 → discovers the WLC (DHCP option 43, DNS name CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER , or broadcast) → builds the CAPWAP tunnel → downloads its configuration → starts its SSIDs. Troubleshooting APs: AP has no power or reduced radios → PoE class or budget (7.4); standalone AP clients get no address in one SSID → that SSID's VLAN missing from the trunk; lightweight AP never joins → no DHCP or route to the WLC, or UDP 5246/5247 blocked; lightweight AP on a trunk with the wrong native VLAN → it gets an address in the wrong subnet.

Two-uplink host using LACP: SW4 Copy commands SW4(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/11 - 12 SW4(config-if-range)# description ESXi-01 vmnic0-1 SW4(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk SW4(config-if-range)# switchport trunk native vlan 999 SW4(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,30,99 SW4(config-if-range)# switchport nonegotiate SW4(config-if-range)# channel-group 11 mode active SW4(config-if-range)# exit SW4(config)# interface port-channel 11 SW4(config-if)# switchport mode trunk SW4(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999 SW4(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,30,99 SW4(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk ! host does not bridge between its NICs Host using independent teaming (no LACP): configure both ports as identical trunks without channel-group , each with spanning-tree portfast trunk . c: Chapter 8 · Validating network documentation with CDP and LLDP
x: A network drawing is correct on the day it is made. Then a technician moves a cable to a spare port, a switch is replaced by a different model, a management address changes — and nobody updates the drawing. Months later someone troubleshoots from the wrong picture. CDP and LLDP let devices describe their own direct connections, so you can check the documentation against what is really cabled. Both are Layer 2 protocols: a device sends periodic advertisements out each interface, and the directly connected neighbor stores them. Advertisements are never forwarded , so a device learns only about its directly connected neighbors ( Figure 8.1 ). They also work only between devices that run the protocol: switches, routers, IP phones and APs do; most PCs and printers do not. Figure 8.1 Discovery scope: each device learns only its directly connected CDP/LLDP neighbors In Figure 8.1 the arrows are advertisements on each link, in both directions. Because DSW1 does not pass SW1's advertisement on to R1, building a full network map means logging in to each device in turn and following the neighbors hop by hop. PC1 is invisible to both protocols, so end hosts are documented from the MAC address table instead. x: CDP runs on Cisco routers, switches, IP phones and APs, and is enabled by default on every interface. CDP version 2 is the default. What CDP advertises: device ID (hostname), management IP address(es), local port the advertisement left from, platform (model), capabilities (router, switch, phone…), software version, and on CDPv2 the native VLAN , duplex , VTP domain, and for phones the voice VLAN and power request. show cdp neighbors — one line per neighbor (Lab 6.1, on DSW1): DSW1 Copy commands DSW1# show cdp neighbors Capability Codes: R - Router, T - Trans Bridge, B - Source Route Bridge S - Switch, H - Host, I - IGMP, r - Repeater, P - Phone, D - Remote, C - CVTA, M - Two-port Mac Relay Device ID Local Intrfce Holdtme Capability Platform Port ID SW1 Gig 1/0/1 155 S I WS-C2960- Gig 0/1 SW1 Gig 1/0/3 155 S I WS-C2960- Gig 0/2 SW2 Gig 1/0/2 161 S I WS-C2960- Gig 0/1 SW2 Gig 1/0/4 161 S I WS-C2960- Gig 0/2 DSW2 Gig 1/0/21 143 R S I WS-C3650- Gig 1/0/21 DSW2 Gig 1/0/22 143 R S I WS-C3650- Gig 1/0/22 R1 Gig 1/0/24 170 R B S I ISR4331 Gig 0/0/0 Column Belongs to Meaning Device ID Neighbor Neighbor's hostname Local Intrfce This device My port the neighbor is connected to Holdtme — Seconds left before the entry expires if no new advertisement arrives Capability Neighbor What the neighbor is (R, S, P…) Platform Neighbor Neighbor's model (often truncated) Port ID Neighbor The neighbor's port at the other end of the cable The classic exam trap: "Local Intrfce" is yours; "Port ID" is the neighbor's. c: Chapter 8 · Validating network documentation with CDP and LLDP
x: LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) does the same job as CDP but is vendor-neutral , so it discovers non-Cisco switches, servers, firewalls and phones. Information is carried in TLVs (type-length-value fields). Mandatory TLVs are chassis ID, port ID and time-to-live; optional ones include system name, system description, system capabilities, port description and management address. On many Cisco IOS devices LLDP is off by default . Turn it on globally; each interface then both transmits and receives unless you say otherwise: DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# lldp run ! enable globally DSW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/24 DSW1(config-if)# no lldp transmit ! stop sending on this port DSW1(config-if)# no lldp receive ! stop listening on this port Command Mode Effect lldp run / no lldp run Global config Enable / disable LLDP lldp transmit / lldp receive Interface config Per-direction control (both on once LLDP runs) lldp timer 30 Global config Advertisement interval (default 30 s) lldp holdtime 120 Global config How long neighbors keep the entry (default 120 s) lldp reinit 2 Global config Delay before LLDP initializes on a port (default 2 s) show lldp Privileged EXEC Status and timers show lldp neighbors [detail] Privileged EXEC Neighbor table / full TLVs show lldp interface Privileged EXEC Per-interface transmit/receive state DSW1 Copy commands DSW1# show lldp neighbors Capability codes: (R) Router, (B) Bridge, (T) Telephone, (C) DOCSIS Cable Device (W) WLAN Access Point, (P) Repeater, (S) Station, (O) Other Device ID Local Intf Hold-time Capability Port ID SW1 Gi1/0/1 120 B Gi0/1 SW2 Gi1/0/2 120 B Gi0/1 R1 Gi1/0/24 120 R Gi0/0/0 ... Total entries displayed: 7 The same rule applies: Local Intf is yours, Port ID is the neighbor's. LLDP capability codes differ from CDP's — a switch is B (bridge), a phone T , an AP W . LLDP-MED (Media Endpoint Discovery) extends LLDP for endpoints such as IP phones: the switch advertises the voice VLAN and QoS settings in a Network Policy TLV, and the phone reports its PoE needs and inventory. It is how non-Cisco phones learn their voice VLAN (Chapter 7). Memory trick C DP is C isco's own; LLDP is the open IEEE 802.1AB version every vendor speaks. Default timers: CDP 60 s / 180 s hold, LLDP 30 s / 120 s hold.

t: 8.5 CDP or LLDP? And when to turn them off
c: Chapter 8 · Validating network documentation with CDP and LLDP
x: Situation Use All-Cisco network CDP (already on); LLDP optional Mixed vendors, servers, Linux hosts LLDP Non-Cisco IP phones LLDP-MED Cisco IP phones CDP (or LLDP-MED) Security. Advertisements reveal hostnames, models, software versions and management IPs — useful to an attacker planning an exploit. Best practice: Disable on ports facing untrusted networks: the Internet edge, ISP links, guest-facing ports ( no cdp enable , no lldp transmit ). Keep them on infrastructure links and on IP phone ports, where the voice VLAN depends on them. Some organisations disable CDP globally and use LLDP only where needed.

x: Figure 8.2 shows the loop. In words: Collect the documentation: topology drawing, port-to-port connection table, IP addressing plan, device inventory (models, software). Gather the evidence on every switch and router: show cdp neighbors detail and/or show lldp neighbors detail , plus show interfaces description and show interfaces status . Compare field by field for every link: neighbor hostname, local port , remote port , platform/model, management IP, and (CDP) native VLAN and duplex. For each mismatch, decide what is wrong. If the network works and follows the design standard, the documentation is wrong: update it. If the documented design is the approved standard (for example a cabling plan), the network is wrong: fix it through change control, then re-check. Hosts that do not run CDP/LLDP (PCs, printers): verify with show mac address-table interface <port> and the DHCP or ARP tables. Publish the corrected documentation with the date and who verified it, and update interface description s so the next audit is faster. Matching links go straight to the published record; mismatches go either to a documentation fix or, when the network breaks the approved design, to a change that is re-checked from step 2.

x: CDP: Cisco proprietary, on by default, every 60 s, holdtime 180 s; CDPv2 adds native VLAN and duplex. cdp run (global), cdp enable (interface). LLDP: IEEE 802.1AB, often off by default on Cisco IOS ( lldp run ), every 30 s, holdtime 120 s, reinit 2 s; per-interface lldp transmit / lldp receive . LLDP-MED gives phones their voice VLAN and PoE information. Scope: directly connected neighbors only; advertisements are never forwarded. PCs and printers usually run neither protocol. Reading output: Local Intrfce / Local Intf = my port; Port ID = the neighbor's port. Each EtherChannel member is listed separately. detail / show cdp entry adds management IP, full platform, software version, native VLAN and duplex. Validation: compare hostname, both ports, model, IP (and VLAN/duplex) for every link; correct whichever side breaks the approved design; verify hosts with MAC, ARP and DHCP tables; publish dated documentation. Security: disable on untrusted or Internet-facing ports; keep on infrastructure links and phone ports. Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea "Port ID is my port" Port ID is the neighbor's port "CDP shows the whole network" Only directly connected neighbors "LLDP works as soon as it is configured on one side" It must run on both ends (transmit on one, receive on the other) "A mismatch means the cabling is wrong" Often the documentation is wrong; check the approved design "CDP can find the printer" Printers and PCs rarely run CDP; use the MAC address table

c: Chapter 9 · Rapid PVST+ and STP protection
x: Redundant links between switches are good: if one fails, another carries traffic. But Ethernet frames have no TTL field , so a frame caught in a Layer 2 loop circulates forever ( Figure 9.1 ). Three things happen within seconds: Figure 9.1 A Layer 2 loop without STP: one broadcast becomes an endless storm In Figure 9.1 the red arrows follow one copy of PC1's broadcast around the triangle. Each switch floods it out every port except the one it arrived on, so it never stops and every lap adds more copies. The numbered effects below happen in parallel. Broadcast storm — every switch floods each broadcast out every other port, so copies multiply until links and CPUs are saturated. MAC address table instability — the same source MAC arrives on different ports, so the switch keeps relearning it ( %SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF ). Duplicate frames — hosts receive multiple copies of the same unicast frame. Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) prevents this by choosing one loop-free tree through the switches and blocking the redundant ports. If an active link fails, STP unblocks a backup path.

c: Chapter 9 · Rapid PVST+ and STP protection
x: Switches running STP exchange BPDUs (Bridge Protocol Data Units) to build the tree. In RSTP every switch sends a BPDU on its designated ports every hello time (2 s) ; a neighbor is considered lost after three missed hellos (6 s). Each BPDU carries the sender's view of who the root is, its cost to reach the root, and its own bridge ID. The bridge ID (BID) is 8 bytes ( Figure 9.2 ): Figure 9.2 Bridge ID structure with a VLAN 10 example Figure 9.2 shows why priorities jump in steps of 4096: the priority has only 4 bits, sitting above the 12-bit VLAN field. IOS prints the two together as one number, which is why VLAN 10's default appears as 32778. Part Bits Meaning Bridge priority 4 Configurable in steps of 4096 : 0, 4096, 8192 … 61440. Default 32768 Extended system ID 12 The VLAN number , added to the priority MAC address 48 A MAC address of the switch (the tie-breaker) So in VLAN 10 a switch with default priority shows 32778 (32768 + 10). Lower BID is better. The priority is compared first; the MAC address decides only when priorities are equal.

Cisco switches commonly use the short method by default; some platforms use the long method ( spanning-tree pathcost method long ). c: Chapter 9 · Rapid PVST+ and STP protection
x: Worked example ( Figure 9.3 ): SW-A, SW-B and SW-C in a triangle, all 1 Gb/s links (cost 4), all at default priority, VLAN 10. MACs: SW-A 0011.1111.1111, SW-B 0022.2222.2222, SW-C 0033.3333.3333. Figure 9.3 STP election result for VLAN 10: root bridge, root ports, designated ports and the alternate port Figure 9.3 is the end state of the four steps below. Every link has exactly one designated port, every non-root switch exactly one root port, and the single leftover port (red) discards. Elect one root bridge per VLAN — lowest BID. All priorities are 32778, so the lowest MAC wins: SW-A is root . Every port on the root bridge is a designated port . Each non-root switch picks one root port — lowest root path cost. SW-B reaches SW-A directly for 4 (via C would be 8): SW-B Gi0/1 is its root port . Likewise SW-C Gi0/1 . Each link (segment) picks one designated port — the side advertising the lowest root path cost. On the SW-B–SW-C link both advertise cost 4, a tie. Break ties in this order: lowest root path cost → lowest sender bridge ID → lowest sender port priority → lowest sender port number. SW-B's BID is lower than SW-C's, so SW-B Gi0/2 is designated . SW-C Gi0/2 is neither root nor designated, so it becomes an alternate port and discards — the loop is broken. Exam method: find the root first; then on each non-root switch find its cheapest path to the root (root port); then on each link the end closer to the root is designated; every port left over is alternate (or backup) and blocks. Common traps The root bridge is chosen by BID, not by speed or position , so an old access switch can become root by accident if nobody sets priorities. Cost is added for the ports a BPDU enters , not exits. Memory trick Every STP tie-break is lowest wins : bridge ID → root path cost → sender bridge ID → sender port ID. Elect the root bridge , then a root port per switch, then a designated port per link — everything left blocks.

t: 9.8 RSTP port states (2.5.b) and rapid convergence
c: Chapter 9 · Rapid PVST+ and STP protection
x: RSTP reduces 802.1D's five states to three: 802.1D state RSTP state Learns MACs? Forwards frames? Disabled Discarding No No Blocking Discarding No No Listening Discarding No No Learning Learning Yes No Forwarding Forwarding Yes Yes Why RSTP is fast: Alternate ports are pre-computed. If the root port fails, the alternate port becomes the root port and starts forwarding immediately. Proposal/agreement handshake. On a point-to-point link a new designated port sends a proposal ; the neighbor syncs its own ports and replies with an agreement , and the port forwards at once instead of waiting through timers. Edge ports (PortFast) go straight to forwarding because nothing can loop through an end host. Faster failure detection: three missed hellos (6 s) instead of the 20 s max age. Link types decide whether the handshake can be used: point-to-point (full-duplex links between switches, the normal case), shared (half duplex, old hubs — falls back to slower timers) and edge (PortFast ports). show spanning-tree prints them in the Type column ( P2p , Shr , P2p Edge ). Timers (defaults): hello 2 s, max age 20 s, forward delay 15 s. RSTP rarely relies on max age and forward delay; you should not need to change any of them for the exam. Memory trick RSTP has only three states — D iscarding, L earning, F orwarding. Discarding absorbs the old blocking, listening and disabled states.

c: Chapter 9 · Rapid PVST+ and STP protection
x: Step 1 — run Rapid PVST+ on every switch. Some platforms default to PVST+ (802.1D); mixing works but loses the rapid behaviour on those links. DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst Step 2 — choose the root bridges deliberately (2.5.a). Put the root on a distribution switch, never leave it to chance: DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10,30 root primary ! DSW1 = root for VLANs 10 and 30 DSW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 40,99 root secondary ! backup root for 40 and 99 DSW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 40,99 root primary DSW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10,30 root secondary root primary is a macro : it sets the priority to 24576, or lower if needed to beat the current root. root secondary sets 28672, so the switch takes over only if the primary fails. Both are one-time calculations written into the configuration as spanning-tree vlan X priority N . You can also set the value directly (multiples of 4096): DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096 Step 3 (optional) — influence the path with cost or port priority on an interface: SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24 SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 40 cost 2 ! make this path cheaper for VLAN 40 SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 40 port-priority 64 ! 0-240 in steps of 16; default 128; lower wins Remember: cost changes the decision on the switch where you configure it (its root port); port priority affects the neighbor's choice, because the neighbor compares the sender's port ID. Command Mode Effect spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst Global Enable Rapid PVST+ spanning-tree vlan <list> root primary / secondary Global Make this switch root / backup root spanning-tree vlan <list> priority <0–61440> Global Set bridge priority (multiple of 4096) spanning-tree vlan <list> cost <n> Interface Override the port cost for those VLANs spanning-tree vlan <list> port-priority <0–240> Interface Override port priority (multiple of 16) spanning-tree pathcost method {short \| long} Global Choose the cost scale Per-VLAN load sharing. With DSW1 root for VLANs 10 and 30 and DSW2 root for 40 and 99, each VLAN builds its own tree, so different VLANs block different links and both distribution switches carry traffic. Align the STP root with the VLAN's default gateway (the SVI or FHRP active router, Chapter 13) so traffic does not take an extra hop.

c: Chapter 9 · Rapid PVST+ and STP protection
x: Without PortFast, a newly connected access port must negotiate or wait before forwarding; a PC may time out on DHCP. PortFast marks a port as an edge port that moves straight to forwarding, because an end host cannot create a loop. SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1 SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast ! one access port SW1(config)# spanning-tree portfast default ! global: all access (non-trunk) ports SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk ! a trunk to a server/hypervisor (Chapter 7) Newer IOS releases use spanning-tree portfast edge , spanning-tree portfast edge default and spanning-tree portfast edge trunk . IOS prints a warning when you enable PortFast, reminding you to use it only on host ports. A PortFast port still sends BPDUs; if it receives one it loses edge status and runs normal STP. Never enable PortFast on a link to another switch.

t: 9.11 BPDU guard, root guard and loop guard (2.5.d)
c: Chapter 9 · Rapid PVST+ and STP protection
x: These three features protect the tree from mistakes and attacks. Figure 9.4 shows where each belongs. Figure 9.4 Placement of root guard, loop guard, PortFast and BPDU guard in the campus In Figure 9.4 each coloured dot marks the port end where a feature is configured, and the text beside each row names it. Root guard sits on the distribution side of the access links, loop guard on the access side of the same links, and PortFast with BPDU guard on every host port. BPDU guard — for edge ports. If any BPDU arrives (someone plugged in a switch), the port is err-disabled immediately. SW1 Copy commands SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable ! per port SW1(config)# spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default ! global: all PortFast ports %SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port Fa0/1 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port. %PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/1, putting Fa0/1 in err-disable state Recover by removing the cause and then shutdown / no shutdown , or automatically with errdisable recovery cause bpduguard and errdisable recovery interval 300 (seconds). Root guard — for designated ports that should never lead toward the root, typically distribution-switch downlinks to access switches. If a superior BPDU (one claiming a better root) arrives, the port is placed in root-inconsistent state (discarding). It recovers automatically when the superior BPDUs stop. DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# interface port-channel 1 DSW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root %SPANTREE-2-ROOTGUARD_BLOCK: Root guard blocking port Port-channel1 on VLAN0010. Loop guard — for root and alternate ports (the uplinks of access switches). If BPDUs stop arriving on such a port — for example because one fibre strand failed and the link is now unidirectional — normal STP would wrongly turn it into a forwarding designated port and create a loop. Loop guard instead puts it in loop-inconsistent state (discarding) until BPDUs return. SW1 Copy commands SW1(config)# spanning-tree loopguard default ! global: all point-to-point ports SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard loop ! or per port Feature Put it on Triggered by Action Recovery PortFast Edge (host) ports — Port forwards immediately — BPDU guard Edge ports Any BPDU received err-disabled Manual bounce or errdisable recovery Root guard Distribution downlinks (designated ports) Superior BPDU received root-inconsistent (discarding) Automatic when superior BPDUs stop Loop guard Access uplinks (root and alternate ports) Missing BPDUs loop-inconsistent (discarding) Automatic when BPDUs resume Root guard and loop guard cannot be enabled on the same port. BPDU filter (stops sending and receiving BPDUs) also exists, but it disables protection and is not a v2.0 objective; avoid it unless a design specifically requires it. show spanning-tree inconsistentports lists ports blocked by root guard or loop guard; show interfaces status err-disabled lists ports shut by BPDU guard.

c: Chapter 9 · Rapid PVST+ and STP protection
x: Loops cause broadcast storms, MAC flapping and duplicate frames because Ethernet has no TTL. STP blocks redundant ports. Rapid PVST+ = one RSTP instance per VLAN. spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst . BID = priority (multiple of 4096, default 32768) + VLAN number + MAC. Lowest wins. VLAN 10 default shows 32778. Election: lowest BID = root (all its ports designated) → each non-root switch's lowest-cost path = root port → each link's lowest-cost side = designated → the rest are alternate (discarding). Ties: root cost → sender BID → sender port priority → sender port number. Costs (short): 10M 100, 100M 19, 1G 4, 10G 2, 2×1G bundle 3. Roles: root, designated, alternate, backup. States: discarding, learning, forwarding. root primary = priority 24576 (or lower); root secondary = 28672. Put roots on distribution switches; share VLANs between them. PortFast on host ports only; BPDU guard err-disables on any BPDU; root guard blocks on a superior BPDU (root-inconsistent, auto-recovers); loop guard blocks when BPDUs stop (loop-inconsistent, auto-recovers). Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea "The fastest or newest switch becomes root" The lowest BID does; set priorities deliberately "The root bridge has a root port" It has none; all its ports are designated "Port priority on my switch changes my root port" Port priority influences the neighbor's choice; use cost to change your own "Root guard and BPDU guard do the same thing" BPDU guard err-disables on any BPDU; root guard blocks only on a superior BPDU and recovers by itself "PortFast is fine on any port" Only on host-facing ports; on a switch link it risks a loop

t: 10.2 How a router forwards a packet
c: Chapter 10 · Interpreting the routing table
x: A router makes the same decision for every packet, independently ( Figure 10.1 ): Figure 10.1 The router's per-packet forwarding process Figure 10.1 follows one packet from arrival to departure. The two red boxes are the only routing reasons to drop it: the TTL ran out, or no route matched. Everything this chapter teaches happens in steps 3 to 5. Receive the frame. Check the FCS; accept it only if the destination MAC is the router's own interface MAC (or broadcast/multicast it listens to). De-encapsulate to the IP packet and decrement the TTL . If TTL reaches 0, drop it and send an ICMP Time Exceeded back to the source (this is how traceroute works). Look up the destination IP in the routing table and choose the longest matching prefix (10.4). No match and no default route? Drop the packet and send ICMP Destination Unreachable. Match found: read the next-hop address and/or exit interface . If the next hop is not directly connected, look it up again (a recursive lookup). Resolve the next hop's MAC with ARP (IPv4) or ND (IPv6). If the destination is on a directly connected network, ARP for the destination itself. Re-encapsulate in a new frame for the exit interface (new source and destination MAC, new FCS) and send it. The routing table (the RIB ) is built by the control plane from connected interfaces, static routes and routing protocols. For speed, the forwarding plane uses a copy optimized for lookups (Cisco Express Forwarding, CEF), but its decisions follow the same table.

t: 10.4 The three decisions, and their order
c: Chapter 10 · Interpreting the routing table
x: Three different rules are often confused. They answer different questions, at different times ( Figure 10.3 ): Rule Question it answers When Compares Administrative distance Several sources offer the same prefix ; which one goes into the table? When building the table Lowest AD Metric One protocol has several paths to the same prefix ; which go in? When building the table Lowest metric; equal metrics all go in (ECMP) Longest prefix match A packet arrives; which installed route does it use? Every packet Most specific (longest) prefix that contains the destination The trap AD and metric never compete across different prefixes. A static route to 10.10.0.0/16 (AD 1) does not beat an OSPF route to 10.10.40.0/24 (AD 110) for traffic to 10.10.40.25. Both are installed, because they are different prefixes, and the packet uses the /24 because it is longer. Figure 10.3 Route selection: AD and metric when building the table, longest match when forwarding Read Figure 10.3 as two separate jobs. The left column runs whenever routing information changes and decides which routes are installed for each prefix. The right column runs for every packet and only ever looks at installed routes, choosing by prefix length alone.

c: Chapter 10 · Interpreting the routing table
x: A route contains a destination if the destination's first n bits equal the route's first n bits, where n is the prefix length. Among all routes that contain the destination, the router uses the one with the largest n . Worked example on R1's table — destination 10.10.40.25 ( Figure 10.4 ): Figure 10.4 Longest prefix match for 10.10.40.25 against five of R1's routes In Figure 10.4 the three filled bars are routes that contain 10.10.40.25; the highlighted one is longest, so it wins. The /30 is longer still but does not contain the address, so length alone is never enough: the route must match first. 0.0.0.0/0 contains everything (0 bits to compare). 10.10.0.0/16: the first 16 bits (10.10) match. Contains it. 10.10.40.0/24: the first 24 bits (10.10.40) match. Contains it. 10.10.30.0/24: the third octet differs (30 ≠ 40). Does not contain it. 10.0.0.4/30: covers only 10.0.0.4–10.0.0.7. Does not contain it. The longest containing prefix is 10.10.40.0/24 → next hop 10.0.0.2, exit G0/0/0 . Quick method: for each candidate, apply the candidate's mask to the destination (Chapter 2 block-size method) and see whether you get the candidate's network address. 10.10.40.25 with /24 → 10.10.40.0 ✓; with /16 → 10.10.0.0 ✓; the longer one wins.

t: 10.6 Administrative distance and metric in action
c: Chapter 10 · Interpreting the routing table
x: AD decides between sources. If R1 also had ip route 10.10.40.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.2 , the static route (AD 1) would replace the OSPF route (AD 110) for that same /24 in the table; the OSPF route stays in the OSPF database as a backup. If the static route were configured with AD 130 (a floating static , Chapter 11), OSPF would stay installed and the static would appear only if OSPF lost the route. Metric decides within one protocol. If OSPF knew two paths to 10.20.0.0/24 with costs 3 and 5, only cost 3 is installed. With two paths of equal cost, both are installed and traffic is shared (equal-cost multipath, ECMP): Copy O 10.20.0.0/24 [110/3] via 10.0.0.6, 00:02:11, Port-channel3 [110/3] via 10.0.0.10, 00:02:11, GigabitEthernet1/0/24 OSPF installs up to four equal-cost paths by default ( maximum-paths changes it). Memory trick Administrative distances to know cold: connected 0 · static 1 · eBGP 20 · EIGRP 90 · OSPF 110 · RIP 120 · iBGP 200 . Lower is more trusted.

t: 10.7 Default routes and the gateway of last resort
c: Chapter 10 · Interpreting the routing table
x: A default route is a route to 0.0.0.0/0 (IPv4) or ::/0 (IPv6). It contains every address but is the least specific possible, so it is used only when nothing longer matches. Typical use: the edge router points the default at the ISP, and internal routers learn or point a default toward the edge. Configured statically: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 (shows as S* ). Learned from a routing protocol (for example O*E2 from OSPF's default-information originate , Chapter 12). Learned from DHCP on an Internet-facing interface (AD 254). Gateway of last resort is 198.51.100.1 to network 0.0.0.0 confirms which default is active. If it says not set , packets with no matching route are dropped with ICMP Unreachable.

t: 10.11 Packet Tracer Lab 10.1 — Reading the campus routing tables (Intermediate)

c: Chapter 10 · Interpreting the routing table
x: Per packet: check frame → decrement TTL (0 = drop, ICMP Time Exceeded) → longest-prefix lookup → no route and no default = drop, ICMP Unreachable → ARP/ND for next hop → new frame. Route line: code, prefix/length, [AD/metric] , via next hop, age, exit interface. C and L lines have no brackets; L = the router's own /32 (or /128). Codes: C, L, S, S* (static default), O, O IA, O E1/E2, D, D EX, R, B. "is variably subnetted" lines are headers, not routes. AD: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, EIGRP external 170, iBGP 200, DHCP default 254, 255 never used. Order of rules: AD (same prefix, different sources) and metric (same prefix, same protocol) decide what is installed ; longest prefix match decides what each packet uses . AD never compares different prefixes. Equal metrics → several via lines (ECMP). Default route 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0; shown as the gateway of last resort; "not set" = no default. IPv6: two-line entries, /128 local routes, link-local next hops with an exit interface. Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea "The static route wins because its AD is lower" Only if it is the same prefix ; otherwise the longer prefix wins "10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted means there is a /8 route" It is a header grouping subnets, not a route "The first matching line is used" The longest matching line is used, wherever it is in the table "Metric 30 from OSPF is worse than metric 2 from RIP" Metrics from different protocols cannot be compared; AD decides "[1/0] means metric 1" 1 is the AD, 0 the metric

c: Chapter 11 · IPv4 and IPv6 static routing
x: A static route is a route you type in by hand. It never changes unless you change it, uses no bandwidth or CPU to maintain, and reveals nothing to neighbors. Use static routes for Avoid static routes when A stub network with one way out (a branch, a home router) Many routers and paths: every change must be made by hand everywhere A default route toward the ISP Paths must change automatically after a failure far away A backup path behind a dynamic protocol (floating static) The network grows often Forcing one specific destination along a chosen path (host route) You cannot document and maintain them reliably The four types in objective 3.2 all use the same command; they differ only in the destination and the AD ( Figure 11.1 ): Type Destination Example Purpose Default route (3.2.a) 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 Anything not otherwise known Network route (3.2.b) A subnet or summary ip route 10.20.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2 A whole remote network Host route (3.2.c) One address: /32 or /128 ip route 10.20.20.10 255.255.255.255 10.0.21.2 One server, a loopback, a special path for one device Floating static (3.2.d) Any prefix, with a higher AD ip route 10.20.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.21.2 200 Backup that appears only when the preferred route disappears Figure 11.1 Default, network, host and floating static routes on R1 (the Lab 11.1 network) Figure 11.1 places all four route types from the table on one network, which you build in Lab 11.1. Each blue arrow is one of R1's static routes, pointing toward the destination it describes; the legend gives the exact route.

c: Chapter 11 · IPv4 and IPv6 static routing
x: Copy ip route <network> <mask> { <next-hop-ip> | <exit-interface> | <exit-interface> <next-hop-ip> } [<AD>] [name <text>] [permanent] Parameter Meaning Common mistake network The destination network (all host bits 0) Typing a host address with a subnet mask: IOS rejects it with %Inconsistent address and mask mask Dotted-decimal mask (not /24 ) Wrong mask covers the wrong range next-hop-ip The neighbor's address on a directly connected subnet Using the router's own address, or a far-away address that has no route exit-interface The local interface to send out of Using it alone on Ethernet (see below) AD 1–255; default 1 Making a backup lower than the route it should back up name A label shown in the configuration — permanent Keeps the route even if the exit interface goes down Black-holes traffic during an outage; rarely wanted All static routes are entered in global configuration mode and appear in the running configuration as ip route ... lines. Three ways to say where to go ( Figure 11.2 ): Figure 11.2 Next-hop, exit-interface and fully specified static routes compared Each row of Figure 11.2 shows the command, the routing table line it produces, and what R1 has to ARP for. The dashed red arrow marks the form to avoid on Ethernet; the highlighted row is the safest form. Next hop only — ip route 10.20.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2 . The router must perform a recursive lookup : it looks up 10.0.12.2 in its own table, finds C 10.0.12.0/30 ... GigabitEthernet0/0/1 , and uses that interface. Shown as S 10.20.20.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2 . Exit interface only — ip route 10.20.20.0 255.255.255.0 GigabitEthernet0/0/1 . Shown as directly connected . On a point-to-point serial link this is fine. On Ethernet the router treats every destination as if it were on the wire and ARPs for each one; it works only if the neighbor answers with proxy ARP , and it fills the ARP cache. Avoid it on Ethernet. Fully specified — ip route 10.20.20.0 255.255.255.0 GigabitEthernet0/0/1 10.0.12.2 . No recursive lookup, and ARP only for the next hop. Recommended on Ethernet, and required in IPv6 when the next hop is a link-local address. When is a static route installed? Only when its next hop is reachable (recursion succeeds) or its exit interface is up. If the exit interface goes down, the route is removed (unless permanent ). This is what makes a floating static take over (11.5).

c: Chapter 11 · IPv4 and IPv6 static routing
x: A floating static is a static route configured with an AD higher than the route it backs up. Because the preferred route has a lower AD, the floating route stays out of the routing table — it "floats" above it — until the preferred route disappears ( Figure 11.3 ). Figure 11.3 Floating static failover on R1: before and after the primary link fails In Figure 11.3 the blue arrow is the route R1 is actually using. On the left the AD 1 route wins and the AD 200 route exists only in the configuration. On the right the primary interface is down, its route is removed, and the floating route is installed with [200/0]. R1 Copy commands R1(config)# ip route 10.20.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2 ! primary, AD 1 R1(config)# ip route 10.20.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.21.2 200 ! backup, AD 200 R2(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.12.1 ! primary default R2(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.21.1 200 ! backup default Choosing the AD: Backing up Floating AD must be higher than Typical choice Another static route 1 5–254 An OSPF-learned route 110 111–254 (often 120–200) An EIGRP-learned route 90 91–254 If the floating route's AD is equal to the primary's, both are installed and traffic is load-shared; if it is lower , the "backup" becomes the primary. Both are classic exam faults. What a floating static can and cannot detect. It takes over when the preferred route is removed : the primary static's exit interface went down (link failure detected locally), or the dynamic protocol withdrew the route. A static route cannot detect a failure further away — for example the ISP's router behind a working link — so it keeps sending traffic into a dead path. Detecting remote failures needs tracking (IP SLA) or a routing protocol, which are beyond objective 3.2. Viewing a floating route. It does not appear in show ip route while unused. Check the configuration ( show running-config | include ip route ) and, after a failure, look for its AD in brackets: S 10.20.20.0/24 [200/0] via 10.0.21.2 . Memory trick A floating static route floats above the primary because its AD is set higher (for example 130, above OSPF's 110). It sinks into the routing table only when the primary route disappears.

(c) host route R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:acad:20::/64 2001:db8:acad:f021::2 200 ! (d) floating static R2(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing R2(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 GigabitEthernet0/0/1 FE80::1 ! default via R1's link-local R2(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 GigabitEthernet0/0/2 FE80::1 200 ! floating default Next-hop form Example Notes Global unicast next hop ipv6 route 2001:db8:acad:20::/64 2001:db8:acad:f012::2 Recursive lookup, as in IPv4 Exit interface only ipv6 route 2001:db8:acad:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0/1 Works on point-to-point links; on Ethernet relies on the neighbor answering ND for every destination Link-local next hop ipv6 route ::/0 GigabitEthernet0/0/1 FE80::1 Interface is mandatory — every link uses FE80::/10. R1 Copy commands R1# show ipv6 route static S ::/0 [1/0] via 2001:DB8:FFFF::1 S 2001:DB8:ACAD:20::/64 [1/0] via 2001:DB8:ACAD:F012::2 S 2001:DB8:ACAD:20::10/128 [1/0] via 2001:DB8:ACAD:F021::2 The floating route is again invisible until the primary route is removed.

c: Chapter 11 · IPv4 and IPv6 static routing
x: IPv4: ip route <network> <mask> {next-hop | exit-int | exit-int next-hop} [AD] . IPv6: ipv6 route <prefix/len> ... [AD] with ipv6 unicast-routing enabled. Next hop only = recursive lookup. Exit interface only = "directly connected"; on Ethernet relies on proxy ARP — avoid. Fully specified = best on Ethernet; mandatory for IPv6 link-local next hops . Default 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 (S*, gateway of last resort). Network route to a subnet or summary. Host route /32 or /128 wins by longest match. Floating static = higher AD than the route it backs up; installed only when that route is removed. Floating AD must exceed: static 1, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110. Equal AD = load sharing; lower = it becomes primary. A static route is installed only if its next hop is reachable / exit interface up; it cannot detect remote failures . Every route needs a return route. Test with ping <dest> source <LAN-IP> and traceroute . Network address must have host bits 0, or IOS says %Inconsistent address and mask . Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea "A floating static shows in show ip route all the time" Only after the preferred route disappears; otherwise check the configuration "Backup route AD 1 makes failover faster" AD 1 equals the primary: both are installed and traffic is load-shared "A ping from the router proves the route works" It may use the router's link address; test from the LAN address "A static route fails over when the ISP fails" Only if the local next hop or interface fails "IPv6 link-local next hops work like global ones" They need the exit interface specified

c: Chapter 12 · Single-area OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
x: Static routes do not scale and cannot react to failures beyond the next hop (Chapter 11). A dynamic routing protocol lets routers tell each other which networks they can reach and recalculate automatically when something changes. OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is an open-standard link-state protocol: every router learns the full map of its area, then each runs the SPF (Dijkstra) algorithm to compute the best (lowest-cost) path to every network. Property OSPF Type Link-state, interior gateway protocol Versions OSPFv2 for IPv4; OSPFv3 for IPv6 Administrative distance 110 Metric Cost = reference bandwidth ÷ interface bandwidth Transport IP protocol 89 Multicast 224.0.0.5 all OSPF routers, 224.0.0.6 DR/BDR (IPv6: FF02::5, FF02::6) Hello / dead timers 10 s / 40 s on broadcast and point-to-point networks Areas Area 0 is the backbone; v2.0 tests single-area OSPF (everything in area 0)

c: Chapter 12 · Single-area OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
x: Discover neighbors with Hello packets on every OSPF-enabled interface. Form adjacencies and exchange the link-state database (LSDB). Each router floods LSAs (link-state advertisements) describing its links; all routers in the area end up with an identical LSDB . Each router runs SPF with itself as the root and installs the best paths as O routes. When a link changes, only the affected LSA is flooded and SPF reruns — fast convergence without periodic full updates. The five OSPF packet types: Type Name Purpose 1 Hello Discover and keep neighbors; carry the parameters that must match 2 DBD (Database Description) Summary list of the LSAs in the sender's database 3 LSR (Link-State Request) Ask for LSAs you are missing 4 LSU (Link-State Update) Carry full LSAs 5 LSAck Acknowledge LSUs

Figure 12.1 OSPF neighbor states and the packets that move two routers from Down to Full Read Figure 12.1 top to bottom: the arrows are packets, the left column is the state they cause. A pair reaches FULL only after both databases match. State Meaning Stuck here usually means Down No Hellos received Link down, OSPF not enabled on the interface, passive interface, ACL blocking 224.0.0.5 Init Hello received, but my RID is not in it One-way communication; Hellos not reaching the other side 2-Way Each sees itself in the other's Hello Normal between two DROthers; otherwise DR/BDR election issue ExStart / Exchange Negotiating and exchanging DBDs MTU mismatch Loading Requesting missing LSAs Corrupt or lost LSUs (rare) Full Synchronized Healthy What must match for two routers to become neighbors (the Hello packet carries these): Area ID (both interfaces in area 0). Subnet and mask on the shared link. Hello and dead intervals . Authentication settings (excluded from the objective, but they must match). Stub area flag (not relevant in a single backbone area). Unique router IDs — two routers with the same RID will not form a proper adjacency. MTU — a mismatch lets them reach ExStart/Exchange but not Full. The interface must not be passive . x: Every OSPF router needs a 32-bit router ID (RID) , written like an IPv4 address. It is chosen once, when the OSPF process starts, in this order: The router-id command (best practice: set it). Otherwise the highest IPv4 address on an up loopback interface. Otherwise the highest IPv4 address on an up physical interface. Changing the RID later requires clear ip ospf process (or a reload) to take effect. OSPFv3 uses the same 32-bit RID; on a router with no IPv4 addresses you must configure router-id manually. x: Network type Default on DR/BDR? Neighbors reach FULL with Broadcast Ethernet Yes The DR and the BDR only Point-to-point Serial (HDLC/PPP); configurable on Ethernet No The single neighbor On a link with only two routers (a /30 or /31 between them) a DR is pointless. Setting ip ospf network point-to-point on both ends skips the election and the wait, so the adjacency forms faster. Both ends must use the same network type; mismatched types can form an adjacency yet produce missing routes.

c: Chapter 12 · Single-area OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
x: On a broadcast network every router would otherwise need a full adjacency with every other router — n(n−1)/2 of them. Instead one Designated Router (DR) and a Backup DR (BDR) are elected, and everyone else ( DROther ) forms FULL adjacencies only with those two ( Figure 12.2 ). Figure 12.2 DR/BDR election on a broadcast LAN: FULL and 2-WAY adjacencies In Figure 12.2 the blue lines are FULL adjacencies; the dashed line between the two DROthers is 2-WAY, which is correct and expected. Election rules: Highest interface OSPF priority wins (0–255, default 1 ; ip ospf priority <n> ). Tie: highest router ID . Priority 0 = never DR or BDR. No preemption : a better router that joins later does not take over until the DR fails or the OSPF process is reset on the segment. When the DR fails, the BDR becomes DR and a new BDR is elected. The election happens per segment (per interface), so a router can be DR on one LAN and DROther on another.

c: Chapter 12 · Single-area OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
x: Cost = reference bandwidth ÷ interface bandwidth , with a default reference of 100 Mb/s . Costs below 1 are rounded up to 1, so FastEthernet, Gigabit and 10-Gigabit links all cost 1 by default — OSPF cannot tell them apart. Fix it on every router with the same value: R1 Copy commands R1(config-router)# auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000 ! in Mb/s: now 10G = 1, 1G = 10, 100M = 100 You can also set a cost directly on an interface: ip ospf cost 20 . The route's metric is the sum of the outgoing interface costs along the path, from the router to the destination.

c: Chapter 12 · Single-area OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
x: Method 1 — network statements in router configuration mode. Each statement uses a wildcard mask (the inverse of a subnet mask: 0 = must match, 1 = ignore) to select interfaces; matching interfaces join the area. R1 Copy commands R1(config)# router ospf 1 ! process ID: local only, need not match R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1 R1(config-router)# auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000 R1(config-router)# network 10.0.123.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 ! the LAN R1(config-router)# network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0 ! the /30 point-to-point link R1(config-router)# network 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 ! the loopback LAN R1(config-router)# passive-interface loopback10 ! advertise it, but send no Hellos R1(config-router)# default-information originate always ! advertise a default route into OSPF Method 2 — per interface (clearer, and the only method in OSPFv3): R1 Copy commands R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/0 R1(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 0 Command Mode Purpose / notes router ospf <pid> Global Starts OSPF process; the process ID is locally significant router-id <a.b.c.d> Router Sets the RID; needs clear ip ospf process if OSPF already runs network <addr> <wildcard> area <id> Router Enables OSPF on matching interfaces. network 10.0.123.1 0.0.0.0 area 0 matches exactly one interface ip ospf <pid> area <id> Interface Enables OSPF on this interface passive-interface <int> / passive-interface default Router No Hellos (no neighbors) on that interface, but its network is still advertised. Use on LAN and loopback interfaces with no routers ip ospf network point-to-point Interface Point-to-point type: no DR/BDR (3.3.b). On a loopback it advertises the real mask instead of /32 ip ospf priority <0-255> Interface DR election priority (3.3.c) ip ospf cost <n> Interface Override the computed cost ip ospf hello-interval / dead-interval Interface Timers; must match neighbors auto-cost reference-bandwidth <Mb/s> Router Same value on every router default-information originate [always] Router Advertise a default route; always even if this router has no default itself Loopbacks and /32. OSPF advertises a loopback as a /32 host route regardless of its mask. To advertise Lo10 as 10.10.10.0/24 (as if it were a LAN), add ip ospf network point-to-point on the loopback.

x: OSPFv3 works the same way (same states, DR/BDR rules, cost and AD) but is enabled per interface, forms neighbors over link-local addresses, and needs IPv6 routing on: R1 Copy commands R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing R1(config)# ipv6 router ospf 1 R1(config-rtr)# router-id 1.1.1.1 ! mandatory if the router has no IPv4 address R1(config-rtr)# auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000 R1(config-rtr)# passive-interface loopback10 R1(config-rtr)# exit R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/0 R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 1 area 0 R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/1 R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 1 area 0 R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf network point-to-point Newer IOS XE releases also offer the address-family syntax ( router ospfv3 1 , address-family ipv6 unicast , interface ospfv3 1 ipv6 area 0 ); both produce the same result. OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 are separate processes with separate neighbor tables and separate DR elections.

t: 13.2 The problem: one gateway per host
c: Chapter 13 · First hop redundancy protocols
x: A host has one default gateway address. In Lab 5.1 every PC in VLAN 10 uses DSW1's SVI, 10.10.10.1. If DSW1 fails, the hosts keep sending off-subnet traffic to 10.10.10.1 and nothing answers — even though DSW2 could route for them. Changing the gateway on every host is not practical, and hosts do not run routing protocols. A first hop redundancy protocol (FHRP) makes two or more routers share a virtual IP address and a virtual MAC address . Hosts use the virtual IP as their gateway. One router actively forwards for it; another stands by and takes over the same addresses if the first fails ( Figure 13.1 ). Figure 13.1 A first hop redundancy group: one virtual gateway shared by an active and a standby router In Figure 13.1 the dashed box is the virtual router that hosts believe they are talking to. The highlighted DSW1 owns it while active; the Hellos let DSW2 notice when DSW1 stops.

c: Chapter 13 · First hop redundancy protocols
x: Routers in the same group exchange Hello (advertisement) messages on the shared subnet. The router with the highest priority becomes active (HSRP) or master (VRRP); a tie is broken by the highest real IP address. The active router answers ARP requests for the virtual IP with the virtual MAC , and forwards frames sent to that MAC. The standby router listens. If Hellos stop for the hold time , it becomes active and sends a gratuitous ARP so switches relearn where the virtual MAC now lives. Hosts notice nothing: the gateway's IP and MAC have not changed. Preemption. If a higher-priority router comes back after a failure, should it take over again? With preempt enabled it does; without it, the current active router keeps the role. HSRP preemption is off by default ; VRRP preemption is on by default . Tracking. A router can lower its own priority when something else fails — for example its uplink toward the core. If DSW1 tracks its uplink and decrements its priority from 110 to 90, DSW2 (100) takes over (with preempt), avoiding a gateway that has no way out.

Version 1 supports groups 0–255 and IPv4 only; version 2 supports groups 0–4095, IPv6 and millisecond timers. The two versions are not compatible, so use the same version on all group members. Matching the group number to the VLAN ID (group 10 on VLAN 10) is a common, readable convention. HSRP states: Initial → Learn → Listen → Speak → Standby or Active. Seeing routers stuck in Speak or both Active usually means they cannot hear each other's Hellos. Memory trick GLBP is the only FHRP with balancing in its name — and the only one that load-balances across routers by default. HSRP and GLBP are Cisco; VRRP is the open standard.

c: Chapter 13 · First hop redundancy protocols
x: Hosts have one default gateway; an FHRP gives a group of routers a shared virtual IP and virtual MAC so the gateway survives a router failure without host changes. One router forwards (HSRP Active , VRRP Master ); another waits (HSRP Standby , VRRP Backup ). Highest priority wins (default 100), tie → highest real IP. Preemption: HSRP off by default, VRRP on. Tracking lowers priority when an uplink fails. Failover = Hellos stop for the hold time → standby takes over → gratuitous ARP updates switch MAC tables. HSRP: Cisco, Hello 3 s / hold 10 s, UDP 1985, v1 224.0.0.2 MAC 0000.0c07.acXX, v2 224.0.0.102 MAC 0000.0c9f.fXXX (IPv6 in v2). VRRP: open standard, 224.0.0.18, protocol 112, MAC 0000.5e00.01XX, virtual IP may be a real address (owner, priority 255). GLBP: Cisco, load balances within one group (AVG + AVFs). Load share by making different routers Active for different VLANs; align with the STP root. Verify: show standby brief , show standby , show vrrp brief ; on hosts, gateway = virtual IP, arp -a shows the virtual MAC. Common conceptual mistakes Mistake Correct idea "Hosts are configured with both routers' addresses" Hosts use only the virtual IP "The standby router forwards half the traffic" Within one HSRP group only the Active router forwards; share load with multiple groups "A recovered higher-priority router always takes over" Only with preempt (off by default in HSRP) "The virtual MAC changes after a failover" It stays the same; only the switch port that owns it changes "HSRP and VRRP can be mixed in one group" They are different protocols and never form one group

x: Typing an address, mask, gateway and DNS server into every PC, phone and laptop is slow and error-prone, and mistakes cause duplicates and wrong gateways (Chapter 2). DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) lets a host ask the network for its settings. A DHCP server keeps pools of addresses and leases them for a set time. Fact Value Transport UDP: server port 67 , client port 68 First messages Broadcast (the client has no address yet) What a client receives Address, mask, default gateway, DNS servers, domain name, lease time, plus optional extras Typical server A Windows/Linux server in larger networks; an IOS router or switch in small sites and labs IPv6 equivalent DHCPv6 and SLAAC (Chapter 3); this chapter is IPv4 only

c: Chapter 14 · DHCPv4 client, server and relay
x: A new client gets its address in four messages, remembered as DORA ( Figure 14.1 ): Figure 14.1 The DHCP DORA exchange between a client and a server on the same subnet In Figure 14.1 time runs downward. The two messages from the client are broadcasts because it has no address yet; the highlighted Acknowledgment is the moment the lease begins. Discover — client → broadcast. Source 0.0.0.0:68, destination 255.255.255.255:67. "Is there a DHCP server?" It carries the client's MAC address. Offer — server → client. Proposes an address (10.10.10.11), mask, gateway, DNS and lease time. Before offering, an IOS server pings the address to make sure no one is using it. Request — client → broadcast . "I accept the offer from server X." It is broadcast so that every server that made an offer learns which one was chosen; the others return their addresses to the pool. Acknowledgment (ACK) — server → client. Confirms the lease. The client then checks the address with ARP (a duplicate triggers a DHCPDECLINE) and starts using it. Other messages: NAK (server refuses a request, for example the client moved to another subnet), DECLINE (client found the offered address already in use), RELEASE (client gives the address back: ipconfig /release ), INFORM (client already has an address and wants only options). Lease timers. At T1 = 50 % of the lease the client renews by unicast with its own server. If that fails, at T2 = 87.5 % it rebinds by broadcast to any server. If the lease expires, it stops using the address and starts again with a Discover. A Windows client that gets no answer at all assigns itself an APIPA address, 169.254.x.x (Chapter 2) — the classic sign of a DHCP failure. Options you should recognise: Option Meaning IOS pool command 1 Subnet mask network <net> <mask> 3 Default gateway (router) default-router 6 DNS servers dns-server 15 Domain name domain-name 51 Lease time lease <days> [hours] [minutes] 43 Vendor-specific, e.g. WLC address for lightweight APs (Chapter 7) option 43 hex … 82 Relay agent information (added by relays and snooping switches, Chapter 23) — 150 (Cisco) / 66 TFTP server for IP phones option 150 ip … Memory trick DORA : Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. Client on UDP 68, server on UDP 67.

Before an Offer, IOS pings the address. If something answers, the address goes into the conflict table ( show ip dhcp conflict ) and is not leased until you clear it with clear ip dhcp conflict * .

c: Chapter 14 · DHCPv4 client, server and relay
x: Discover messages are broadcasts, and routers do not forward broadcasts . If the DHCP server sits in another subnet — usual in any real network — the router facing the clients must relay the request ( Figure 14.2 ): Figure 14.2 DHCP relay: the client's broadcast becomes a unicast to the server, stamped with giaddr In Figure 14.2 the grey legs are on the client's VLAN and the highlighted legs cross the routed network. The three cards show what is in the packet at each stage; the giaddr value is what lets one central server serve many VLANs. The client broadcasts its Discover in VLAN 10. The relay agent (the SVI or router interface with ip helper-address ) receives it. The relay writes its own interface address in the client VLAN into the giaddr (gateway IP address) field, for example 10.10.10.2, and unicasts the message to the server. The server uses giaddr to choose the pool: the pool whose network contains 10.10.10.2 is STAFF. The server unicasts the Offer back to giaddr; the relay sends it on to the client in VLAN 10. Request and Ack follow the same path. DSW1 Copy commands DSW1(config)# interface vlan 10 DSW1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.0.0.1 ! the DHCP server's address; one line per server Where it goes: on the interface that receives the client's broadcast — the client VLAN's SVI (or router subinterface) — never on the interface toward the server. With HSRP (Chapter 13), configure it on both distribution switches; each relays, the server answers both, and the client takes one Offer. Requirements: the server needs a route back to every giaddr subnet, and a pool whose network contains each giaddr. ip helper-address also forwards a few other UDP broadcast services by default (such as TFTP, DNS and NetBIOS), which matters only when you use them.

x: DORA: Discover (broadcast) → Offer → Request (broadcast) → Ack. Server UDP 67 , client UDP 68 . Also NAK, DECLINE, RELEASE, INFORM. Lease: renew by unicast at T1 = 50 % , rebind by broadcast at T2 = 87.5 % . No server at all → Windows uses 169.254.x.x (APIPA). IOS server: ip dhcp excluded-address (global) + ip dhcp pool with network , default-router , dns-server , domain-name , lease . The server pings before offering; answered addresses go to show ip dhcp conflict . Relay: ip helper-address <server> on the client-facing interface/SVI; the relay fills giaddr with its own interface IP and unicasts to the server; the server picks the pool whose network contains giaddr and needs a route back . IOS client: ip address dhcp on the interface; default gateway installed as AD 254 ; show dhcp lease . c: Chapter 15 · The troubleshooting toolkit
x: Ping says whether a destination answers; traceroute shows the path and where it stops. It relies on the TTL field ( Figure 15.2 ): Figure 15.2 How traceroute discovers each hop with rising TTL values Figure 15.2 runs top to bottom in time. Each probe travels one router further than the last before its TTL runs out, and the router where it dies reveals itself in the reply. The source sends probes with TTL 1 . The first router decrements TTL to 0, drops the probe and returns ICMP Time Exceeded from its own address — that is hop 1. Probes with TTL 2 reach the second router, which returns Time Exceeded — hop 2. TTL keeps rising until a probe reaches the destination , which answers differently (ICMP Port Unreachable for UDP probes, Echo Reply for ICMP probes) and the trace ends. Each hop is normally probed three times, so you see three round-trip times per line. Implementation Probe type Cisco IOS traceroute UDP to high ports (starting at 33434) Linux / macOS traceroute UDP by default ( -I for ICMP) Windows tracert ICMP Echo Request terminal Copy commands C:\> tracert 192.0.2.8 Tracing route to 192.0.2.8 over a maximum of 30 hops 1 1 ms <1 ms <1 ms 10.10.10.2 2 1 ms 1 ms 1 ms 10.0.0.1 3 2 ms 1 ms 1 ms 192.0.2.8 Trace complete. Note hop 1: the real address of DSW1 (10.10.10.2), not the HSRP virtual IP — the Active router answers from its own interface address. DSW1 Copy commands DSW1# traceroute 10.20.20.1 Type escape sequence to abort. Tracing the route to 10.20.20.1 1 10.0.0.1 1 msec 1 msec 0 msec 2 198.51.100.1 1 msec 1 msec 1 msec 3 198.51.100.2 2 msec 1 msec 1 msec 4 198.51.100.1 2 msec 2 msec 1 msec 5 198.51.100.2 2 msec 2 msec 2 msec ... The same two addresses alternating is a routing loop : R1 sends 10.20.20.0/24 to the ISP by its default route, and the ISP sends it back by its 10.0.0.0/8 route. Neither has a specific route, so the packet bounces until TTL expires. Traceroute shows Meaning * No reply within the timeout for that probe * * * from some hop onward The path stops there: the next router has no route, a filter drops probes, or replies cannot get back !H / !N / !P Host / network / protocol unreachable returned !A Administratively prohibited — an ACL rejected it (Chapter 20) Repeating addresses Routing loop Final hop never reached, but ping works Probes (UDP high ports) filtered while ICMP Echo is allowed Traceroute shows the forward path only. The return path may differ (asymmetric routing), so a stop at hop n can also mean hop n cannot route its Time Exceeded back to you.

c: Chapter 16 · Wireless principles
x: A wireless LAN (WLAN) carries Ethernet-like frames over radio. The access point (AP) is the bridge between the radio and the wired network. Term Meaning SSID The network name users see (up to 32 characters), for example Staff-WiFi BSS (basic service set) One AP radio and the clients associated to it BSSID The MAC address of that AP radio — identifies the BSS ESS (extended service set) Several APs advertising the same SSID on the same network, so clients roam between them IBSS (ad hoc) Clients talking directly with no AP Association A client joining a BSS (after authentication) Beacon Frame an AP broadcasts about 10 times a second to advertise its SSIDs and capabilities Wi-Fi is half duplex and shared. Only one station can transmit on a channel at a time, so 802.11 uses CSMA/CA (collision avoidance ): listen before sending, wait a random back-off, and expect an acknowledgment for every unicast frame. More clients and more APs on the same channel mean more waiting. Standard Wi-Fi name Bands Maximum data rate (theoretical) 802.11b — 2.4 GHz 11 Mb/s 802.11a — 5 GHz 54 Mb/s 802.11g — 2.4 GHz 54 Mb/s 802.11n Wi-Fi 4 2.4 and 5 GHz 600 Mb/s 802.11ac Wi-Fi 5 5 GHz about 6.9 Gb/s 802.11ax Wi-Fi 6 / 6E (6E adds 6 GHz) 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz about 9.6 Gb/s 802.11be Wi-Fi 7 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz about 46 Gb/s Real throughput is far lower — often less than half — because of the shared medium, protocol overhead and distance. Faster standards rely on wider channels, more spatial streams (MIMO: several antennas sending different data at once) and denser modulation, which need a strong, clean signal.

c: Chapter 16 · Wireless principles
x: A band is a range of frequencies; a channel is a slice of a band that one BSS uses. Which channels you may use, and at what power, is set by each country's regulator — always check local rules (in Nepal, the Nepal Telecommunications Authority). 2.4 GHz 5 GHz 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E / 7) Channels 1–13 in most countries (1–11 in the USA), 5 MHz apart, each about 20–22 MHz wide About 25 non-overlapping 20 MHz channels (36–165), grouped into U-NII bands Up to 59 non-overlapping 20 MHz channels where the full band is allowed Non-overlapping Only 1, 6 and 11 All of them at 20 MHz All of them Range / penetration Longest, best through walls Shorter Shortest Interference Crowded: neighbours, Bluetooth, microwave ovens Much less; some channels need DFS (avoid radar) Very little; only new devices; WPA3 required Typical use Coverage, old and IoT devices Most enterprise traffic High-density, high-speed areas Why 1, 6 and 11? A 2.4 GHz channel is about 22 MHz wide but channels are only 5 MHz apart, so neighbouring channel numbers overlap ( Figure 16.1 ). Channels five apart do not overlap, which leaves three usable channels in most of the world. Figure 16.1 2.4 GHz channels 1–13 and why only 1, 6 and 11 avoid overlap Figure 16.1 draws every 2.4 GHz channel to scale on one frequency axis. The three highlighted arcs never touch each other, while each grey arc overlaps one or two of them. Channel width. 802.11n and later can bond adjacent 20 MHz channels into 40, 80, 160 (and on Wi-Fi 7, 320) MHz channels. Wider channels carry more data but leave fewer separate channels for neighbouring APs. In 2.4 GHz use 20 MHz only; in busy 5 GHz offices 20 or 40 MHz is common; 6 GHz has room for 80 MHz and wider. Choosing channels for several APs ( Figure 16.2 ): Neighbouring APs use different, non-overlapping channels; reuse a channel only for APs far enough apart not to hear each other strongly. On 2.4 GHz, alternate 1, 6, 11 in a honeycomb pattern. Set transmit power so cells overlap by roughly 15–20 % for roaming — not more; louder is not better. Prefer 5 GHz (and 6 GHz) for clients; consider turning off some 2.4 GHz radios in dense areas. In a controller-based WLAN, Radio Resource Management (RRM) on the WLC chooses channels and power automatically and adapts to interference. Figure 16.2 A 2.4 GHz channel reuse plan with channels 1, 6 and 11 Figure 16.2 is the honeycomb from step 2: each colour is one channel, and wherever two cells overlap they carry different channels, so neighbours never take turns on the same frequency. Two failures of channel planning are tested often: co-channel interference (APs on the same channel hear each other and must take turns — capacity drops, but nothing is corrupted) and adjacent-channel interference (APs on overlapping channels such as 1 and 3 corrupt each other's frames — worse). Memory trick The only non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels: 1, 6 and 11 .

c: Chapter 16 · Wireless principles
x: Radio frequency (RF) signals are electromagnetic waves. Term Meaning Frequency Cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). Wi-Fi uses 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz Wavelength Length of one cycle: about 12.5 cm at 2.4 GHz, 6 cm at 5 GHz. Shorter waves lose strength faster and pass through obstacles less well Amplitude Signal strength Modulation How data is encoded on the wave; denser modulation (more bits per symbol) needs a cleaner signal Power and decibels. Wireless power is tiny and spans a huge range, so it is expressed in dBm — decibels relative to 1 milliwatt. Rule Example 0 dBm = 1 mW — +3 dB doubles the power, −3 dB halves it 20 dBm = 100 mW, 17 dBm = 50 mW +10 dB is ten times the power, −10 dB a tenth 10 dBm = 10 mW, −10 dBm = 0.1 mW Received Wi-Fi signals are negative dBm −65 dBm is stronger than −80 dBm Signal quality measures: Measure Meaning Typical guidance RSSI (received signal strength) How strong the AP's signal is at the client, in dBm −67 dBm or better for voice and video; −70 dBm adequate for data; −80 dBm poor Noise floor Background RF energy on the channel Often about −90 to −95 dBm SNR (signal-to-noise ratio) Signal minus noise, in dB 25 dB or more good; below 15 dB unreliable Example: RSSI −65 dBm with a noise floor of −92 dBm gives SNR = 27 dB — good. The same RSSI next to a microwave oven raising the noise to −75 dBm gives only 10 dB, and the connection struggles even though the "bars" look full. How signals behave on the way: Effect What happens Example Free-space path loss Signal weakens with distance (faster at higher frequency) 5 GHz cells are smaller than 2.4 GHz cells Absorption Material soaks up energy Water, people, concrete walls Reflection Signal bounces off smooth surfaces Metal cabinets, glass, lift shafts Refraction Signal bends passing between materials Air layers, glass Scattering Signal spreads in many directions Rough surfaces, foliage, dust Diffraction Signal bends around an obstacle, leaving an RF shadow behind it Corners, pillars Multipath Copies arrive by different paths at slightly different times Reflections indoors; MIMO turns it into an advantage, older radios suffer Antennas and EIRP. An omnidirectional antenna radiates in all horizontal directions (ceiling APs); a directional antenna (patch, Yagi, dish) focuses energy one way for corridors, warehouses or point-to-point bridges. Antenna gain is in dBi . The power that actually leaves the antenna is EIRP = transmitter power + antenna gain − cable loss : for example 17 dBm + 6 dBi − 2 dB = 21 dBm. Regulators limit EIRP, not just transmitter power.
